fields.description:
{{doPutConnectorConfig}} needs two requests to complete its job, which means another user’s request could slip in between and cause a race condition. For example, the first request sets initial offsets, but the second doesn’t. When the race happens, the connector created by the second request could use the initial offsets set by the first request without any warning.

Of course ... if both requests have identical initial offsets, that is fine 🙂

fields.description:
[KIP-1306|https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/spaces/KAFKA/pages/406623733/KIP-1306+Extend+ConsumerRebalanceListener+with+Consumer-Aware+methods] added {{RebalanceListener}}, whose callbacks receive a  {{RebalanceConsumer}}: a restricted view of the consumer that only allows operations that are safe during a rebalance.

KAFKA-20684 moved {{WorkerSinkTask}}'s rebalance handling onto {{RebalanceListener}}, but it still ignores the {{RebalanceConsumer}} and uses the task's own consumer. Connector code that runs during the rebalance ({{SinkTask.open()}} and {{close()}}) also reaches the consumer directly through {{WorkerSinkTaskContext}}.

Connect should use the {{RebalanceConsumer}} for everything it does during a rebalance
fields.summary: Use RebalanceConsumer in WorkerSinkTask rebalance callbacks

fields.description:
While remote storage is disabled for a topic, maybeIncrementLogStartOffset advances only logStartOffset, so retention and DeleteRecords leave localLogStartOffset behind. When remote.storage.enable is then set to true, nothing advances it. localLogStartOffset stays below logStartOffset until the broker restarts or an uploaded segment is deleted locally.

In the meantime, ListOffsets returns wrong values:
* EARLIEST_LOCAL_TIMESTAMP returns the stale localLogStartOffset, which is below logStartOffset.
* EARLIEST_PENDING_UPLOAD_TIMESTAMP returns -1 although nothing has been uploaded yet.

Repro (unit test against UnifiedLog on trunk): segments [0,5) [5,10) [10,15) with remote storage disabled, DeleteRecords to 7, then enable remote storage. Result: logStartOffset=7, localLogStartOffset=0, EARLIEST_LOCAL=0, EARLIEST_PENDING_UPLOAD=-1. After a restart, both return 7.

Disabling remote storage already handles the opposite direction: ConfigHandler advances logStartOffset to localLogStartOffset. Enabling it could do the same for localLogStartOffset.
fields.summary: localLogStartOffset is not advanced when remote storage is enabled on an existing topic

fields.description:
We landed the first version of the refiner w/o any JMH results. If we need to optimize for better performance a few ideas to explore (some already discussed during code review):
 * replace Java Streams API usage with “native” loops

 * replace list+sort with heap

 * cache more helper data structures (cf below)

 * maybe integrate deeper with reconciler

About helper data structures: currently, the GC uses an in-memory cache to store the intermediate assignment. We could extent this, to also store helper data structures like “load index” which change incrementally for most cases, and we should be able to re-used across refiner runs (atm, the refiner computes all helpers from scratch on each run). Other candidates for caching is “funding candidate order” (ie, in which order we plan to assign warmup tasks — it’s mainly load based so keeping it across refiner runs and maintaining it incrementally might also cut costs; for this case, a heap might become really beneficial).

fields.summary: Remove unused javax jaxb-api and activation dependencies

renderedFields.description:
javax.activation:activation and javax.xml.bind:jaxb-api are declared in a few places in build.gradle with the comment

Jersey dependency that was available in the JDK before Java 9

This is a stale comment as Jersey is 3.1.x uses the jakarta namespace and already resolves (transitively) com.sun.activation:jakarta.activation and jakarta.xml.bind:jakarta.xml.bind-api.

In Kafka 4.0 the project was migrated to Jakarta with KIP-1032 and KAFKA-16437 so the two remaining javax dependencies should be safe to remove. Verified with :trogdor:test, :connect:mirror:test (including
the MirrorMaker integration tests) and the :connect:runtime REST tests.

Next to the benefit of handling less dependencies we can remove 3 jars from the released artifact and shave off around ~247 KB in size.

  • jaxb-api-2.3.1.jar
  • activation-1.1.1.jar
  • javax.activation-api-1.2.0.jar

Note that in theory there can be a few connector which relied on having jaxb and activation on the classpath from Kafka. However KIP-1032 already calls out this scenario

Users that use the Connect framework will need to upgrade their custom connectors to use the new jakarta namespace (if they rely on it) or else will need to use an isolated classloader.

fields.description:
A standby task whose state store uses the input topic as its changelog may only apply records up to the offset committed by the active task. This happens for {{builder.table(topic)}} when {{topology.optimization}} is set to {{all}} or {{reuse.ktable.source.topics}}; without this optimization the store has its own changelog topic and is not affected.

{{StoreChangelogReader}} keeps fetching beyond the committed offset, and the records that cannot be applied yet stay in {{ChangelogMetadata#bufferedRecords}}. Nothing pauses the partition, so the buffer grows with every poll.

When the active task is far behind the end of the input topic, for example when the application starts on a topic that already holds a lot of data, the standby buffers almost the whole backlog and can run out of memory.

Before 2.5.0, {{StreamThread}} paused a standby partition when {{StandbyTask#update}} returned records beyond the offset limit, and resumed it after they were applied. This behavior was lost in the refactoring of KAFKA-9113, so 2.5.0 and later versions are affected.

*Reproduction*
Setup: one broker, two application instances, {{num.standby.replicas=1}}, {{topology.optimization=all}}, a topology with {{builder.table(inputTopic)}}, an active task slowed down by a sleep in a downstream processor, and the instance with the standby task in its own JVM with {{-Xmx192m}}.
* One input partition, 300,000 records of 1 KB: the standby fails with {{OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space}} after about 5 seconds, with about 139,000 records in the restore buffer.
* Eight input partitions, 12,000 records of 50 KB (about 600 MB): the standby fails with {{OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space}} after about 8 seconds, with about 2,250 records (about 113 MB) in the restore buffers of its standby partitions.

The same behavior can be shown without an OOM. With {{restore.consumer.max.poll.records=100}} and {{commit.interval.ms=100}}, the active instance is paused with {{KafkaStreams#pause()}} (so the committed offset does not move) and 10,000 new records are written to the input topic. Within a few seconds the restore consumer of the standby instance fetched 8,703 of them ({{records-consumed-total}}), although it could not apply any of them.

Other cases do not grow: a standby with its own changelog topic, and an active task that is restoring (records that can be applied are applied right after they are fetched).

*Proposed fix*
Pause such a changelog partition while its buffer holds records beyond the limit offset, and resume it once the limit has moved past them. This restores the behavior from before KAFKA-9113 and adds no new config or public API. The restore buffer then holds at most one poll of records per partition ({{max.poll.records}}), and the restore consumer keeps at most one fetch per partition (about {{max.partition.fetch.bytes}}) until the partition is resumed.

The cost: when the committed offset of the active task moves, the standby applies the records it already has and then needs one more fetch for the rest.

Related: KAFKA-19992 / KIP-1325 proposes a configurable limit for the restore buffer. The two changes are independent.
fields.summary: Standby task with source-topic changelog fetches and buffers records beyond the committed-offset limit without bound

comments.body:
Logs from the two reproductions in the description, on trunk at commit 4a8164b8. In both runs the standby instance runs in its own JVM with {{-Xmx192m -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError}}, and the active task processes about 1,300 records per second.

Attached:
* {{standby-trunk-oom-1-partition-1kb.log}}: one input partition, 300,000 records of 1 KB.
* {{standby-trunk-oom-8-partitions-50kb.log}}: eight input partitions, 12,000 records of 50 KB.
* {{CdcStandbyOomTest.java}}: the test that produced the first run. It uses {{EmbeddedKafkaCluster}} and starts the standby with {{ProcessBuilder}}, so it can be dropped into {{streams/integration-tests}}. It is a measurement, not a test for the PR.

First run, the standby instance sampled every 500 ms. {{fetched}} is {{records-consumed-total}} of its restore consumer, {{applied}} is the sum of {{batchSize}} from {{StandbyUpdateListener#onBatchLoaded}}:
{noformat}
t_ms,fetched,applied,waiting,heap_used_mb,heap_max_mb,active_tasks,standby_tasks
3027,0,0,0,47,192,0,0
3528,17085,7620,9465,78,192,0,1
4029,99495,7620,91875,163,192,0,1
4531,148740,10050,138690,183,192,0,1
{noformat}

End of the standby's log:
{noformat}
[2026-10-14 13:22:58,057] INFO [Consumer clientId=app-cdc-oom-...-StateUpdater-1-restore-consumer, groupId=null] Assigned to partition(s): cdc-oom-0 (org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.ClassicKafkaConsumer:647)
...
Terminating due to java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
{noformat}

With the fix from the PR, the same run finished all 300,000 records in about 186 seconds, and the standby's heap usage stayed at or below 67 MB.

Before 2.5.0, {{StreamThread}} paused a standby partition when {{StandbyTask#update}} returned records beyond the offset limit, and resumed it after they were applied. This behavior was lost in the refactoring of KAFKA-9113, so 2.5.0 and later versions are affected.

*Reproduction*
Setup: one broker, two application instances, {{num.standby.replicas=1}}, {{topology.optimization=all}}, a topology with {{builder.table(inputTopic)}}, an active task slowed down by a sleep in a downstream processor, and the instance with the standby task in its own JVM with {{-Xmx192m}}.
* One input partition, 300,000 records of 1 KB: the standby fails with {{OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space}} after about 5 seconds, with about 139,000 records in the restore buffer.
* Eight input partitions, 12,000 records of 50 KB (about 600 MB): the standby fails with {{OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space}} after about 8 seconds, with about 2,250 records (about 113 MB) in the restore buffers of its standby partitions.

The same behavior can be shown without an OOM. With {{restore.consumer.max.poll.records=100}} and {{commit.interval.ms=100}}, the active instance is paused with {{KafkaStreams#pause()}} (so the committed offset does not move) and 10,000 new records are written to the input topic. Within a few seconds the restore consumer of the standby instance fetched 8,703 of them ({{records-consumed-total}}), although it could not apply any of them.

Other cases do not grow: a standby with its own changelog topic, and an active task that is restoring (records that can be applied are applied right after they are fetched).

*Proposed fix*
Pause such a changelog partition while its buffer holds records beyond the limit offset, and resume it once the limit has moved past them, as before 2.5.0. The restore buffer then holds at most one poll of records per partition ({{max.poll.records}}), and the restore consumer keeps at most one fetch per partition (about {{max.partition.fetch.bytes}}) until the partition is resumed.

The cost: when the committed offset of the active task moves, the standby applies the records it already has and then needs one more fetch for the rest.

Related: KAFKA-19992 / KIP-1325 proposes a configurable limit for the restore buffer. The two changes are independent.

fields.description:
The Docker image can only run controllers with static voters. With controller.quorum.bootstrap.servers instead:
 # KafkaDockerWrapper always formats with plain kafka-storage format. On a controller without voters, StorageTool requires --standalone or --no-initial-controllers, so the format fails and the container exits.
 # The image configure script rejects KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS on controller-only nodes, but a dynamic voter needs an advertised controller endpoint.

We should (i.) add a new env var (e.g. STORAGE_FORMAT_ARGS) appended to the images format command and (ii.) allow KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS on controllers when it lists only controller listeners.

Default behaviour stays unchanged. Since the env vars are part of the images, interface (KIP-975), this might require a small KIP.

Affects the 3.9.x+ version.

fields.description:
When a member using {{group.protocol=consumer}} or {{group.protocol=streams}} leaves its group, the coordinator cancels the member’s session timer before persisting the member removal records.

If the subsequent local append to {{__consumer_offsets}} fails, the coordinator’s snapshot rollback restores the member metadata, existing assignment, and ownership state. However, session timers are not managed by the snapshot mechanism, so the canceled timer is not restored.

As a result, the coordinator retains a member that has already shut down as the owner of Consumer partitions or Streams active tasks, but no longer has a session timer to expire that member. Even after the append failure is resolved and other members continue sending successful heartbeats, the departed member’s partitions or tasks may remain unreleased, leaving processing stalled.

The two protocols use different leave handlers, but share the same underlying cause: timers are canceled before persistence and are not restored on rollback.

 

*Scenario*
 # Dynamic members A and B belong to the same group, with stable assignments. In a Consumer group, A consumes P0 and B consumes P1. In a Streams group, A and B belong to different processes: A processes active task {{{}0_0{}}}, and B processes active task {{{}0_1{}}}.
 # A shuts down and sends a heartbeat with {{memberEpoch=-1}} using the corresponding protocol. A sends no further heartbeats. For Streams, this is an ordinary member departure without requesting application-wide shutdown.
 # The coordinator generates A’s removal records and a group epoch update record, then calls {{cancelTimers()}} to cancel A’s timers before persisting the records.
 # The local append of the batch containing these records fails. The coordinator remains ACTIVE without reloading and performs a snapshot rollback.
 # A’s member metadata and existing partition or active task ownership are restored, but A’s session timer is not.
 # The cause of the append failure is resolved. B continues sending successful heartbeats and processing its existing partitions or tasks, but B’s heartbeats refresh only B’s own session timer.
 # A is not removed even after its session timeout has elapsed. Consumption of P0 remains stalled in the Consumer group, or processing of task {{0_0}} remains stalled in the Streams group.

Even if a subsequent rebalance changes the target assignment to move the affected partition or task to B, B may be unable to acquire it while the coordinator still retains A’s current ownership.

For Streams, this scenario does not require a stateful topology, standby or warm-up replicas, or a custom assignor.

 

*Conditions that can cause the append failure*

One possible path is a reduction of {{max.message.bytes}} for {{__consumer_offsets}} between batch creation and append. Both group types use the same coordinator runtime persistence path, so this condition applies to both.

The coordinator runtime uses the size limit in effect when creating a batch. If the limit is subsequently reduced and the actual size of the batch containing A’s leave records exceeds the new limit, the log append can fail with {{{}RecordTooLargeException{}}}.

In this failure path, rolling back the batch does not necessarily reload the coordinator. Restoring the size limit allows subsequent writes to succeed, but does not restore A’s canceled session timer.

 

*Impact*

In Consumer groups, consumption of the departed member’s partitions may remain stalled. In Streams groups, input processing for the departed member’s active tasks may remain stalled. Other members can continue processing the partitions or tasks they already own, so the issue does not necessarily stop processing across the entire group.

Reloading the coordinator can register the members’ session timers again. This is therefore not permanent log corruption, but restoring successful writes and waiting for the session timeout are insufficient to guarantee that the affected partitions or tasks will be released.

fields.summary: SslTransportLayer.transferFrom sends stale buffer contents after a failed file read

comments.body: [~mykytab] : Thanks for reporting this. This does seem like a real bug. Your proposed solution seems reasonable.

[~junrao]: Thanks, Jun. The fix is in https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23832: it flips the buffer whether or not the read succeeds, so the buffer holds exactly what was read, and nothing after a failed read.
merged the PR to trunk

renderedFields.description:
When TLS is enabled, SslTransportLayer.transferFrom copies records from the segment into fileChannelBuffer and writes that buffer to the TLS stream. The buffer is cleared before each read:

if (!fileChannelBuffer.hasRemaining()) {
    fileChannelBuffer.clear();
    ...
    int bytesRead = fileChannel.read(fileChannelBuffer, pos);
    if (bytesRead <= 0)
        break;
    fileChannelBuffer.flip();
}
int networkBytesWritten = write(fileChannelBuffer);

If the read throws, or returns no bytes, the buffer is left cleared instead of empty: hasRemaining() is true and the buffer still holds the previous chunk. When something was already written in the same call, the IOException is swallowed (if (totalBytesWritten > 0) return totalBytesWritten). The next call then skips the read, writes the stale buffer to the socket as the next chunk of the file, advances the position, and fails on the following read the same way. A read error on the segment never surfaces; the rest of the requested region is sent as copies of an earlier chunk.

Reproduced on trunk (03e6606430): one controller and three brokers, JDK 17, Linux 6.8, the leader's log directory on dm-dust. The tail of a 10 MiB segment is made unreadable while its head stays in the page cache, then a consumer reads the partition from the beginning over the SSL listener. On the broker's network thread:

pread64(176, ..., 32768, 2850816) = 16384
pread64(176, ..., 32768, 2867200) = -1 EIO (Input/output error)

followed by 168 more -1 EIO at offsets advancing by 32768, covering the whole 5.5 MiB region. The broker logs nothing about it: no exception, no disconnect, the log directory stays online and the leader is unchanged. The consumer gets 5456 of 20000 records, then:

Record batch for partition t1-0 at offset 5456 is invalid, cause: Record is corrupt (stored crc = 1243940787, computed crc = 114489509)

The same scenario over the PLAINTEXT listener surfaces the error: sendfile returns EIO and the broker closes the connection with java.io.IOException: Input/output error.

Impact:

  • Clients and followers on a TLS listener receive bytes that are not in the file. The CRC check catches it, so a readable record on healthy replicas is reported as corrupt, and the partition cannot be consumed past it from this leader.
  • Disk read errors on TLS listeners never reach the code that handles I/O errors, so KAFKA-16304 cannot work for TLS until this is fixed.
  • The stale bytes come from an earlier transfer on the same connection, so nothing from another connection is exposed.

The bytesRead <= 0 branch leaves the buffer in the same state; FileRecords.writeTo's size check usually rejects a truncated file before that is reached.

Proposed fix: leave the buffer empty when a read does not succeed (for example set its limit to 0 when the read throws or returns no bytes), so the next call reads again and the original IOException propagates.

Disclosure per the ASF generative tooling guidance: the reproduction and the analysis were produced with AI assistance; I have reviewed and am responsible for all of it.

junrao: Thanks, Jun. The fix is in https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23832: it flips the buffer whether or not the read succeeds, so the buffer holds exactly what was read, and nothing after a failed read.
merged the PR to trunk

comments.body: Happy to work on this issue, thanks!
Can this only happen in the test or in prodcution as well? If the latter, this should probably be a bug ticket not a test ticket

In production, {{TaskManager.shutdown()}} is only called from {{{}StreamThread#completeShutdown(){}}}. This happens either on the stream thread itself after its run loop exits, or from {{StreamThread#shutdown()}} when the thread is still in the {{CREATED}} state and was never started. In either case, no other thread is accessing the {{TaskManager}} concurrently.

The race comes from the test teardown, which calls {{thread.taskManager().shutdown(false)}} from the test thread while the {{StreamThread}} may still be running and picking up restored tasks from the StateUpdater. Production code never shuts down the {{TaskManager}} from another thread like this, so I think fixing the test is right.
thanks!

comments.body: Hi [~yuzhou], I can take a look

This seems like a genuine bug. As mentioned in the description Kafka has some restrictions on certain config value changes. While the broker is running, going from {{num.io.threads}} 16->8->6 pass the validation check "{_}value should be at least half the current value{_}". However after the restart the situation changes:
 # After startup the broker first operates with the static config from server.properties (16)
 # In the meantime the broker looks at the metadata log and tries to replay it on top of the latest checkpoint
 # When the replay is finished all intermediate edits are collapsed to their final values. (change num.io.threads->8 is lost)
 # Since we only have the final value (6) DynamicConfigPublisher tries to update num.io.threads 16-> 6 which fails the "{_}value should be at least half the current value{_}". check.

Bug also affects other configs with similar restrictions:
||Config||Validation site||Checked against||Example (static -> persisted dynamic)||
|num.io.threads|DynamicThreadPool (broker and controller)|current KafkaConfig value|16 -> 6|
|num.replica.fetchers|DynamicThreadPool|current KafkaConfig value|16 -> 6|
|num.recovery.threads.per.data.dir|DynamicThreadPool|current KafkaConfig value|16 -> 6|
|background.threads|DynamicThreadPool|current KafkaConfig value|16 -> 6|
|num.network.threads|Acceptor.validateReconfiguration (SocketServer.scala)|processors.length (running processor count)|16 -> 6|
|log.cleaner.threads|LogCleaner.validateReconfiguration|config.numThreads|16 -> 6|
|mirror.num.replica.fetchers|DynamicClusterMirrorConfig|current broker config|16 -> 6|
|remote.log.reader.threads|DynamicRemoteLogConfig|server.config value|16 -> 6|

After more investigation it looks like a very similar problem already came up in KAFKA-17431. As a solution brokers now use the latest metadata snapshot for bootstrap instead of the static config. comments.body: Hi yuzhou, I can take a look

This seems like a genuine bug. As mentioned in the description Kafka has some restrictions on certain config value changes. While the broker is running, going from num.io.threads 16->8->6 pass the validation check "value should be at least half the current value". However after the restart the situation changes:

  1. After startup the broker first operates with the static config from server.properties (16)
  2. In the meantime the broker looks at the metadata log and tries to replay it on top of the latest checkpoint
  3. When the replay is finished all intermediate edits are collapsed to their final values. (change num.io.threads->8 is lost)
  4. Since we only have the final value (6) DynamicConfigPublisher tries to update num.io.threads 16-> 6 which fails the "value should be at least half the current value". check.

Bug also affects other configs with similar restrictions:

Config Validation site Checked against Example (static -> persisted dynamic)
num.io.threads DynamicThreadPool (broker and controller) current KafkaConfig value 16 -> 6
num.replica.fetchers DynamicThreadPool current KafkaConfig value 16 -> 6
num.recovery.threads.per.data.dir DynamicThreadPool current KafkaConfig value 16 -> 6
background.threads DynamicThreadPool current KafkaConfig value 16 -> 6
num.network.threads Acceptor.validateReconfiguration (SocketServer.scala) processors.length (running processor count) 16 -> 6
log.cleaner.threads LogCleaner.validateReconfiguration config.numThreads 16 -> 6
mirror.num.replica.fetchers DynamicClusterMirrorConfig current broker config 16 -> 6
remote.log.reader.threads DynamicRemoteLogConfig server.config value 16 -> 6
remote.log.manager.copier.thread.pool.size DynamicRemoteLogConfig server.config value 16 -> 6
remote.log.manager.expiration.thread.pool.size DynamicRemoteLogConfig server.config value 16 -> 6
remote.log.manager.follower.thread.pool.size DynamicRemoteLogConfig remoteLogManagerFollowerThreadPoolSize(), which can fall back to remote.log.manager.thread.pool.size 16 -> 6

fields.description:
KAFKA-19804 initializes the heartbeat interval to request.timeout.ms to prevent busy polling while the first heartbeat is in flight. However, this can delay fatal error reporting in the share consumer.

ShareConsumerImpl.pollForFetches() waits for up to the minimum of maximumTimeToWait() and the remaining poll timeout. If the first heartbeat returns a fatal error, such as GROUP_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED, the network thread enqueues an error event, but BackgroundEventHandler does not wake the fetch buffer. The application thread processes the error only after its current fetch-buffer wait finishes.

With the default request.timeout.ms and a sufficiently long poll timeout, this can delay reporting an already received error by approximately 30 seconds.

AsyncKafkaConsumer already caps the fetch-buffer wait at retryBackoffMs when no partitions are assigned. The share consumer has no equivalent cap.

h1. Kafka licenses/ folder audit
 

The {{licenses/}} folder shipped in the Kafka binary distribution has drifted from the dependencies it covers: one referenced file is missing, one has the wrong license text, four ship for nothing, and several copyright lines are stale. CI only compares versions in {{{}LICENSE-binary{}}}, never the contents of {{{}licenses/{}}}.
h2. Findings

16 files in {{licenses/}} were compared with the {{LICENSE-binary}} references and with the license each dependency ships at its current version ({{{}gradle/dependencies.gradle{}}}).
||#||File / entry||Problem||Fix||
|1|{{jakarta.activation-2.0.1}} → {{licenses/jakarta-BSD-3-clause}}|Referenced file does not exist. The jar's own {{META-INF/LICENSE.md}} is EDL 1.0 (BSD-3, Copyright 2018 Oracle).|Point to {{licenses/eclipse-distribution-license-1.0}}|
|2|{{protobuf-java-BSD-3-clause}}|Wrong text: "Copyright 2023, the original author or authors" (jline's wording). Upstream v25.5 is "Copyright 2008 Google Inc."|Replace with upstream v25.5 {{LICENSE}}|
|3|{{mock-oauth2-server-MIT}}|Test-only dependency ({{{}testImplementation{}}}), not bundled|Delete|
|3|{{jsr305-BSD-3-clause}}|Dependency dropped from {{LICENSE-binary}} in 2025, file left behind|Delete|
|3|{{paranamer-BSD-3-clause}}|Same as jsr305|Delete|
|3|{{eclipse-distribution-license-1.0}}|Not referenced, although it is the right file for #1 and #4|Reference it|
|4|{{{}jakarta.activation-api-2.1.0{}}}, {{jakarta.xml.bind-api-3.0.1}}|Listed as CDDL 1.1 + GPLv2; POM and jar say EDL 1.0|Move to an EDL 1.0 section|
|4|{{jakarta.servlet-api-6.0.0}}|Listed as CDDL 1.1 + GPLv2; POM says EPL 2.0 / GPL2 w/ CPE|Move to the EPL 2.0 section|
|4|{{CDDL+GPL-1.1}}|Unreferenced once the three jars above move|Delete|
|5|{{classgraph-MIT}} (4.8.196)|2019 vs upstream 2026|Upstream text|
|5|{{slf4j-MIT}} (1.7.36)|2004-2017 QOS.ch vs 2004-2022 QOS.ch Sarl (Switzerland)|Upstream text|
|5|{{jline-BSD-3-clause}} (3.30.17)|2002-2018 vs 2002-2023|Upstream text|
|5|{{jopt-simple-MIT}} (5.0.4)|2004-2016 vs 2004-2015 at the tag|Upstream text|
|5|{{argparse-MIT}} (0.7.0)|2011-2017 vs 2011, 2014, 2015 at the tag|Upstream text|
|5|{{zstd-jni-BSD-2-clause}} (1.5.7-17)|Extra title line; "BSD License" vs "BSD-2-Clause License" + URL|Upstream text|
|–|{{{}pcollections-MIT{}}}, {{{}hdrHistogram-BSD-2-clause{}}}, {{{}re2j-GO{}}}, {{eclipse-public-license-2.0}}|Match upstream|None|
h2. Proposed change

One {{MINOR}} PR, branch {{{}MINOR-fix-licenses-folder{}}}, touches only {{LICENSE-binary}} and {{{}licenses/{}}}.
 * {{{}LICENSE-binary{}}}: replace the "CDDL 1.1 + GPLv2" section with an "Eclipse Distribution License - v 1.0" section ({{{}jakarta.activation-2.0.1{}}}, {{{}jakarta.activation-api-2.1.0{}}}, {{{}jakarta.xml.bind-api-3.0.1{}}}); add {{jakarta.servlet-api-6.0.0}} to the EPL 2.0 section; drop the broken {{jakarta-BSD-3-clause}} line.
 * Replaced with upstream text at the current version: {{{}protobuf-java-BSD-3-clause{}}}, {{{}classgraph-MIT{}}}, {{{}slf4j-MIT{}}}, {{{}jline-BSD-3-clause{}}}, {{{}jopt-simple-MIT{}}}, {{{}argparse-MIT{}}}, {{{}zstd-jni-BSD-2-clause{}}}.
 * Deleted: {{{}mock-oauth2-server-MIT{}}}, {{{}jsr305-BSD-3-clause{}}}, {{{}paranamer-BSD-3-clause{}}}, {{{}CDDL+GPL-1.1{}}}.

h2. Verification

A fresh {{./gradlew clean releaseTarGz}} on the fix branch confirms the change.
 * The third-party jars in {{libs/}} match the entries in {{LICENSE-binary}} exactly. Nothing is missing on either side.
 * Every {{licenses/...}} path in {{LICENSE-binary}} exists, and every file in {{licenses/}} is referenced.
 * {{jakarta.servlet-api}} is bundled at 6.0.0, as {{LICENSE-binary}} says, even though {{dependencies.gradle}} declares 6.1.0. The 6.1.0 declaration does not reach the runtime classpath.
 * The tarball's {{licenses/}} now holds 12 files, down from 16.

h2. How it drifted

Each problem traces back to one commit. The CI step {{committer-tools/verify_license.py}} (KAFKA-17607) only matches jar names in {{libs/}} against {{{}LICENSE-binary{}}}, so none of these failed a build.
||Date||Commit||What happened||
|2026-05-07|KAFKA-20555 (#22232)|Removed the EDL 1.0 section and moved {{jakarta.activation-api}} and {{jakarta.xml.bind-api}} under CDDL|
|2025-06-12|KAFKA-19153 (#19938)|Added {{mock-oauth2-server-MIT}} for a test-only dependency|
|2025-02-18/19|#18943, #18950|Removed paranamer and jsr305 from {{{}LICENSE-binary{}}}, left their files|
|2025-01-01|KAFKA-18375 (#18359)|Added {{jakarta.activation-2.0.1}} pointing to the non-existent {{{}licenses/jakarta-BSD-3-clause{}}}, and {{jakarta.servlet-api-6.0.0}} under CDDL next to {{javax.servlet-api-3.1.0}}|
|2023-11-29|#14833|Added {{protobuf-java-BSD-3-clause}} with generic wording instead of Google's text|
|2021-04-06|KAFKA-12602 (#10474)|Added argparse and jopt-simple texts copied from newer upstream releases than the bundled jars. Later version bumps of slf4j, jline and classgraph never refreshed their texts|

2 protobuf-java-BSD-3-clause Wrong text: "Copyright 2023, the original author or authors" (jline's wording). Upstream v25.5 is "Copyright 2008 Google Inc." Replace with upstream v25.5 LICENSE
3 mock-oauth2-server-MIT Test-only dependency (testImplementation), not bundled Delete
3 jsr305-BSD-3-clause Dependency dropped from LICENSE-binary in 2025, file left behind Delete
3 paranamer-BSD-3-clause Same as jsr305 Delete
3 eclipse-distribution-license-1.0 Not referenced, although it is the right file for #1 and #4 Reference it
4 jakarta.activation-api-2.1.0, jakarta.xml.bind-api-3.0.1 Listed as CDDL 1.1 + GPLv2; POM and jar say EDL 1.0 Move to an EDL 1.0 section
4 jakarta.servlet-api-6.0.0 Listed as CDDL 1.1 + GPLv2; POM says EPL 2.0 / GPL2 w/ CPE Move to the EPL 2.0 section
4 CDDL+GPL-1.1 Unreferenced once the three jars above move Delete
5 classgraph-MIT (4.8.196) 2019 vs upstream 2026 Upstream text
5 slf4j-MIT (1.7.36) 2004-2017 QOS.ch vs 2004-2022 QOS.ch Sarl (Switzerland) Upstream text
5 jline-BSD-3-clause (3.30.17) 2002-2018 vs 2002-2023 Upstream text
5 jopt-simple-MIT (5.0.4) 2004-2016 vs 2004-2015 at the tag Upstream text
5 argparse-MIT (0.7.0) 2011-2017 vs 2011, 2014, 2015 at the tag Upstream text
5 zstd-jni-BSD-2-clause (1.5.7-17) Extra title line; "BSD License" vs "BSD-2-Clause License" + URL Upstream text
– pcollections-MIT, hdrHistogram-BSD-2-clause, re2j-GO, eclipse-public-license-2.0 Match upstream None

Proposed change

One MINOR PR, branch MINOR-fix-licenses-folder, touches only LICENSE-binary and licenses/.

  • LICENSE-binary: replace the "CDDL 1.1 + GPLv2" section with an "Eclipse Distribution License - v 1.0" section (jakarta.activation-2.0.1, jakarta.activation-api-2.1.0, jakarta.xml.bind-api-3.0.1); add jakarta.servlet-api-6.0.0 to the EPL 2.0 section; drop the broken jakarta-BSD-3-clause line.
  • Replaced with upstream text at the current version: protobuf-java-BSD-3-clause, classgraph-MIT, slf4j-MIT, jline-BSD-3-clause, jopt-simple-MIT, argparse-MIT, zstd-jni-BSD-2-clause.
  • Deleted: mock-oauth2-server-MIT, jsr305-BSD-3-clause, paranamer-BSD-3-clause, CDDL+GPL-1.1.

Verification

A fresh ./gradlew clean releaseTarGz on the fix branch confirms the change.

  • The third-party jars in libs/ match the entries in LICENSE-binary exactly. Nothing is missing on either side.
  • Every licenses/... path in LICENSE-binary exists, and every file in licenses/ is referenced.
  • jakarta.servlet-api is bundled at 6.0.0, as LICENSE-binary says, even though dependencies.gradle declares 6.1.0. The 6.1.0 declaration does not reach the runtime classpath.
  • The tarball's licenses/ now holds 12 files, down from 16.

How it drifted

Each problem traces back to one commit. The CI step committer-tools/verify_license.py (KAFKA-17607) only matches jar names in libs/ against LICENSE-binary, so none of these failed a build.

Date Commit What happened
2026-05-07 KAFKA-20555 (#22232) Removed the EDL 1.0 section and moved jakarta.activation-api and jakarta.xml.bind-api under CDDL
2025-06-12 KAFKA-19153 (#19938) Added mock-oauth2-server-MIT for a test-only dependency
2025-02-18/19 #18943, #18950 Removed paranamer and jsr305 from LICENSE-binary, left their files
2025-01-01 KAFKA-18375 (#18359) Added jakarta.activation-2.0.1 pointing to the non-existent licenses/jakarta-BSD-3-clause, and jakarta.servlet-api-6.0.0 under CDDL next to javax.servlet-api-3.1.0
2023-11-29 #14833 Added protobuf-java-BSD-3-clause with generic wording instead of Google's text
2021-04-06 KAFKA-12602 (#10474) Added argparse and jopt-simple texts copied from newer upstream releases than the bundled jars. Later version bumps of slf4j, jline and classgraph never refreshed their texts

It still checks for {{powered-by.html}} to decide if the path given is actually kafka-site, and it dumps everything into a flat {{kafka-site/<version>/}} dir — neither of those exist anymore now that kafka-site is Hugo-based ({{{}content/en/<version>{}}} for markdown, {{static/<version>}} for javadoc/images). So right now {{stage-docs}} either bails on the sentinel check or writes docs somewhere Hugo never looks at.|

fields.description:
When a workflow references a GitHub Action that isn’t on the ASF org-level allowlist, the job dies at startup with no logs and the PR can still look green — nothing actually ran. We’ve been finding out about this the hard way, after the fact, when a pin drifts off the approved list.

ASF Infra ships a composite action for exactly this — {{{}apache/infrastructure-actions/allowlist-check{}}}— that scans every {{uses:}} ref under {{.github/}} and checks it against the approved allowlist (with the GitHub/ASF-owned orgs {{{}actions/{}}}, {{{}github/{}}}, {{apache/*}} implicitly trusted). It also warns when an approved pin is nearing its upstream expiry, which is the usual cause of the silent failures.

This adds a small workflow wiring that action in, so we catch an unapproved or expiring action at PR time instead of mid-CI. It runs on PRs and on a weekly schedule — the schedule covers the case where an allowlisted pin expires upstream in a week where we don’t touch {{{}.github/{}}}.

Already in use across other ASF projects (Storm,Lucene, Iceberg), and Infra auto-PRs it into major repos, so this just brings Kafka in line with the standard setup.

ASF workflow template 

[https://github.com/apache/infrastructure-actions/blob/main/allowlist-check/README.md]

It also warns when an approved pin is nearing its upstream expiry, which is the usual cause of the silent failures.

This adds a small workflow wiring that action in, so we catch an unapproved or expiring action at PR time instead of mid-CI. It runs on PRs and on a weekly schedule — the schedule covers the case where an allowlisted pin expires upstream in a week where we don’t touch {{{}.github/{}}}.

Already in use across other ASF projects (Storm,Lucene, Iceberg), and Infra auto-PRs it into major repos, so this just brings Kafka in line with the standard setup.

fields.description:
The client configs sasl.login.connect.timeout.ms and sasl.login.read.timeout.ms are optional, defined without defaults in the code, and set only when defined by the app, here [https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/8e65883c1255f93361bbf29efa8425e30b40c5ec/clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/security/oauthbearer/internals/secured/HttpJwtRetriever.java#L212-L216] 

KIP-768 does define default values for them (10000 ms), but the implementation does not seem to consider them, so if not set by the app, calls to the token endpoint would run without explicit boundaries I expect (so hang if the token endpoint does not respond promptly). 

Login calls are triggred from the clients constructors, so I expect the hang could happen when creating them (this login [https://github.com/apache/kafka/blob/8e65883c1255f93361bbf29efa8425e30b40c5ec/clients/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/common/security/authenticator/LoginManager.java#L69])

This Jira is to review this path and fix by applying the defaults proposed by KIP-798.

fields.description:
When a transaction is aborted during partial task revocation in exactly-once mode, processing results can be lost if a retained task is recreated before its pending offset reset is applied.

Records processed in the aborted transaction must be reprocessed from the last committed offset. However, if the pending reset information is lost with the old task instance, the replacement task continues from the consumer’s current position. A subsequent commit can advance the committed offset past the skipped records, preventing normal recovery from reprocessing them.

This violates {*}exactly-once semantics{*}, as some input records never have their processing results committed.

The following scenario illustrates the issue:
 # *Task A and Task B run on the same StreamThread.*
 ## Task B’s committed offset is {{{}100{}}}. It processes records at offsets {{{}100–109{}}}, advancing the consumer position to {{{}110{}}}.
 ## The outputs for these records belong to a transaction that has not yet been committed.
 # *The transaction is aborted while only Task A is revoked.*
 ## rebalance revokes Task A while retaining Task B. During revocation handling, {{sendOffsetsToTransaction()}} times out, and the transaction is aborted.
 ## Task B’s outputs for offsets {{100–109}} are therefore not committed. Task B must reprocess those records starting from committed offset {{{}100{}}}.
 ## Task B is moved into the pending-initialization state, and the partitions requiring an offset reset are recorded in the existing task instance. The consumer position remains at {{{}110{}}}.
 # *Another assignment is handled before Task B resets its offsets.*
 ## Assignment handling closes the existing Task B awaiting initialization and creates a replacement with the same TaskId.
 ## If the pending reset information is not transferred to the replacement task, it does not rewind the consumer to offset {{{}100{}}}. Instead, it continues processing from offset {{{}110{}}}.
 # *A subsequent transaction commits a higher offset.*
 ## The replacement Task B processes the record at offset {{110}} and commits the next offset, {{{}111{}}}.
 ## The processing results for offsets {{100–109}} were discarded by the earlier abort, and those records were never reprocessed. Since the committed offset has advanced to {{{}111{}}}, subsequent restarts or reassignments do not replay them.

The expected behavior is for the replacement task to resume from offset {{{}100{}}}, reprocess the records from the aborted transaction, and commit their results.

Instead, processing can continue past offsets {{{}100–109{}}}, permanently omitting their committed processing results despite exactly-once mode being enabled.
fields.summary: Pending offset resets are lost during task recreation, causing missing processing results under exactly-once semantics

renderedFields.description:
When a transaction is aborted during partial task revocation in exactly-once mode, processing results can be lost if a retained task is recreated before its pending offset reset is applied.

Records processed in the aborted transaction must be reprocessed from the last committed offset. However, if the pending reset information is lost with the old task instance, the replacement task continues from the consumer’s current position. A subsequent commit can advance the committed offset past the skipped records, preventing normal recovery from reprocessing them.

This violates exactly-once semantics, as some input records never have their processing results committed.

The following scenario illustrates the issue:

  1. Task A and Task B run on the same StreamThread.
    1. Task B’s committed offset is 100. It processes records at offsets 100–109, advancing the consumer position to 110.
    2. The outputs for these records belong to a transaction that has not yet been committed.
  2. The transaction is aborted while only Task A is revoked.
    1. rebalance revokes Task A while retaining Task B. During revocation handling, sendOffsetsToTransaction() times out, and the transaction is aborted.
    2. Task B’s outputs for offsets 100–109 are therefore not committed. Task B must reprocess those records starting from committed offset 100.
    3. Task B is moved into the pending-initialization state, and the partitions requiring an offset reset are recorded in the existing task instance. The consumer position remains at 110.
  3. Another assignment is handled before Task B resets its offsets.
    1. Assignment handling closes the existing Task B awaiting initialization and creates a replacement with the same TaskId.
    2. If the pending reset information is not transferred to the replacement task, it does not rewind the consumer to offset 100. Instead, it continues processing from offset 110.
  4. A subsequent transaction commits a higher offset.
    1. The replacement Task B processes the record at offset 110 and commits the next offset, 111.
    2. The processing results for offsets 100–109 were discarded by the earlier abort, and those records were never reprocessed. Since the committed offset has advanced to 111, subsequent restarts or reassignments do not replay them.

The expected behavior is for the replacement task to resume from offset 100, reprocess the records from the aborted transaction, and commit their results.

Instead, processing can continue past offsets 100–109, permanently omitting their committed processing results despite exactly-once mode being enabled.

 ## Assignment handling closes the existing Task B awaiting initialization and creates a replacement with the same TaskId.
 ## If the pending reset information is not transferred to the replacement task, it does not rewind the consumer to offset {{{}100{}}}. Instead, it continues processing from offset {{{}110{}}}.
 # *A subsequent transaction commits a higher offset.*
 ## The replacement Task B processes the record at offset {{110}} and commits the next offset, {{{}111{}}}.
 ## The processing results for offsets {{100–109}} were discarded by the earlier abort, and those records were never reprocessed. Since the committed offset has advanced to {{{}111{}}}, subsequent restarts or reassignments do not replay them.

The expected behavior is for the replacement task to resume from offset {{{}100{}}}, reprocess the records from the aborted transaction, and commit their results.

Instead, processing can continue past offsets {{{}100–109{}}}, permanently omitting their committed processing results despite exactly-once mode being enabled.
This issue links to "GitHub Pull Request #23848 (Web Link)"

GitHub PR is ready for review: [https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23770]

GitHub PR is (finally :))ready for review: [https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23770]
Gradle 9.8.2 was just released so I'll bump PR version: https://github.com/gradle/gradle/releases/tag/v9.8.2

Note: this is also addressing security advisory: Failure to disable repositories failing to establish an SSL connection can expose builds to malicious artifacts

When resolving dependencies, Gradle searches repositories in declaration order. If it encounters connection errors, Gradle will disable the repository and fail dependency resolution. This is necessary for both reproducibility and security reasons to prevent dependencies from being resolved from other repositories without warning.

Scope:

  • Upgrades Gradle from 9.7.1 to 9.8.1 ( ⚠️ addresses https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-j5m7-59rp-24f5)

(!) Note: this is also addressing security advisory: *Failure to disable repositories failing to establish an SSL connection can expose builds to malicious artifacts*
{quote}_When resolving dependencies, Gradle searches repositories in declaration order. If it encounters connection errors, Gradle will disable the repository and fail dependency resolution. This is necessary for both reproducibility and security reasons to prevent dependencies from being resolved from other repositories without warning._

*Scope:*

{quote}_When resolving dependencies, Gradle searches repositories in declaration order. If it encounters connection errors, Gradle will disable the repository and fail dependency resolution. This is necessary for both reproducibility and security reasons to prevent dependencies from being resolved from other repositories without warning._

*Scope:*

(!) Note: this is also addressing security advisory: *Failure to disable repositories failing to establish an SSL connection can expose builds to malicious artifacts*
{quote}_When resolving dependencies, Gradle searches repositories in declaration order. If it encounters connection errors, Gradle will disable the repository and fail dependency resolution. This is necessary for both reproducibility and security reasons to prevent dependencies from being resolved from other repositories without warning._
{quote}
*Scope:*
 * Upgrades Gradle from 9.7.1 to 9.8.1 ( ⚠️ addresses [https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-j5m7-59rp-24f5])
 * Fetches the Gradle wrapper jar from a pinned Gradle commit: because {{v9.8.1}} tag contains a jar that doesn't match the published 9.8.1 checksum

issuetype.description: A problem which impairs or prevents the functions of the product.
issuetype.name: Bug

fields.description:
When the Streams group coordinator rolls back a task assignment change, member assignments and the process ownership index for standby and warm-up tasks can become inconsistent.

In addition to per-member assignments, the coordinator maintains a set of process IDs that own each task. This index prevents the same task from being assigned to different members within the same process in conflicting roles.

Although the ownership index is stored in a {{{}TimelineHashMap{}}}, its values are ordinary {{HashSet}} instances that are mutated in place. Reverting to a snapshot therefore does not restore the previous contents of these sets. Member assignments are restored correctly, but the index may retain ownership from a rolled-back assignment or lose ownership that should have been restored.

A representative scenario involves a log append failure while adding a standby owner to a task that already has one:
 # P1 owns active task T, P3 owns standby task T, and P2 has no assigned tasks.
 # Increasing the number of standby replicas produces a target assignment that also assigns standby T to P2.
 # While processing P2’s heartbeat, the coordinator replays the current-assignment record in memory, changing the standby ownership index to {{{}{P3, P2}{}}}.
 # The log append fails and the coordinator rolls back. P2’s assignment becomes empty again, but P2 remains in the ownership index.
 # If P1 and P3 subsequently leave and P2 needs to receive active T, the coordinator blocks the assignment because it believes another member in process P2 still owns standby T.

No actual owner exists to release the task. The member can continue sending successful heartbeats while retaining an empty assignment and remaining in {{{}UNRELEASED_TASKS{}}}. For an application with a single task, this can halt input processing.

Removing the original member and rejoining with the same process ID may not resolve the issue. Since the original member’s assignment is empty after rollback, member removal does not clean up the stale ownership entry. Restarting an application with persistent stores while preserving its state directory can reuse the same process ID and meet this condition.

The reverse inconsistency can also occur. If a standby or warm-up owner is removed and that change is rolled back, the member’s assignment is restored, but its process ID may remain absent from the ownership index. The check that should prevent another member in the same process from receiving the active task can then incorrectly allow the assignment.

The impact can persist after such a rollback while the same coordinator state remains loaded. Reconstructing coordinator state from persisted member records also rebuilds the ownership index.
fields.summary: Streams group task ownership index is not rolled back, blocking valid task assignments

When the Streams group coordinator rolls back a task assignment change, member assignments and the process ownership index for standby and warm-up tasks can become inconsistent.

In addition to per-member assignments, the coordinator maintains a set of process IDs that own each task. This index prevents the same task from being assigned to different members within the same process in conflicting roles.

Although the ownership index is stored in a TimelineHashMap, its values are ordinary HashSet instances that are mutated in place. Reverting to a snapshot therefore does not restore the previous contents of these sets. Member assignments are restored correctly, but the index may retain ownership from a rolled-back assignment or lose ownership that should have been restored.

A representative scenario involves a log append failure while adding a standby owner to a task that already has one:

  1. P1 owns active task T, P3 owns standby task T, and P2 has no assigned tasks.
  2. Increasing the number of standby replicas produces a target assignment that also assigns standby T to P2.
  3. While processing P2’s heartbeat, the coordinator replays the current-assignment record in memory, changing the standby ownership index to {{{} {P3, P2}

    {}}}.

  4. The log append fails and the coordinator rolls back. P2’s assignment becomes empty again, but P2 remains in the ownership index.
  5. If P1 and P3 subsequently leave and P2 needs to receive active T, the coordinator blocks the assignment because it believes another member in process P2 still owns standby T.

No actual owner exists to release the task. The member can continue sending successful heartbeats while retaining an empty assignment and remaining in UNRELEASED_TASKS. For an application with a single task, this can halt input processing.

Removing the original member and rejoining with the same process ID may not resolve the issue. Since the original member’s assignment is empty after rollback, member removal does not clean up the stale ownership entry. Restarting an application with persistent stores while preserving its state directory can reuse the same process ID and meet this condition.

The reverse inconsistency can also occur. If a standby or warm-up owner is removed and that change is rolled back, the member’s assignment is restored, but its process ID may remain absent from the ownership index. The check that should prevent another member in the same process from receiving the active task can then incorrectly allow the assignment.

The impact can persist after such a rollback while the same coordinator state remains loaded. Reconstructing coordinator state from persisted member records also rebuilds the ownership index.

fields.description:
With the KIP-1071 Streams Rebalance Protocol, when the assignment interval delays a new assignment computation, the coordinator returns {{ASSIGNMENT_DELAYED}} while retaining the existing assignment.

Upon receiving this status, {{StreamsMembershipManager}} sets {{isGroupReady=false}} regardless of whether the member already has assigned tasks. Even when the task assignment is unchanged, the readiness change triggers an assignment callback, and {{DefaultStreamsRebalanceListener}} forwards the updated readiness to the StreamThread.

The default StreamThread processing loop returns before processing records when readiness is false. Consequently, existing tasks that could continue processing are temporarily stopped while the next assignment computation is deferred.

A possible scenario is:
 # Member A has assigned tasks and is processing normally.
 # Member B joins, increasing the group epoch and requiring a new assignment computation.
 # The assignment interval has not elapsed since the last computation, so the coordinator retains the existing target assignment. Member B waits without a target assignment.
 # Member A sends a heartbeat during the same delay window. The coordinator retains A’s existing assignment but also returns {{{}ASSIGNMENT_DELAYED{}}}.
 # Member A sets readiness to false and stops processing its existing tasks.
 # Processing resumes after A receives a heartbeat response without the delay status and completes the assignment callback.

This introduces an unnecessary processing gap despite unchanged task ownership, potentially increasing record processing latency and reducing throughput. The default processing loop also skips punctuation and the commit stage for that iteration.
fields.summary: Streams Group Assignment delays temporarily stop processing existing Streams tasks

renderedFields.description:
With the KIP-1071 Streams Rebalance Protocol, when the assignment interval delays a new assignment computation, the coordinator returns ASSIGNMENT_DELAYED while retaining the existing assignment.

Upon receiving this status, StreamsMembershipManager sets isGroupReady=false regardless of whether the member already has assigned tasks. Even when the task assignment is unchanged, the readiness change triggers an assignment callback, and DefaultStreamsRebalanceListener forwards the updated readiness to the StreamThread.

The default StreamThread processing loop returns before processing records when readiness is false. Consequently, existing tasks that could continue processing are temporarily stopped while the next assignment computation is deferred.

A possible scenario is:

  1. Member A has assigned tasks and is processing normally.
  2. Member B joins, increasing the group epoch and requiring a new assignment computation.
  3. The assignment interval has not elapsed since the last computation, so the coordinator retains the existing target assignment. Member B waits without a target assignment.
  4. Member A sends a heartbeat during the same delay window. The coordinator retains A’s existing assignment but also returns ASSIGNMENT_DELAYED.
  5. Member A sets readiness to false and stops processing its existing tasks.
  6. Processing resumes after A receives a heartbeat response without the delay status and completes the assignment callback.

This introduces an unnecessary processing gap despite unchanged task ownership, potentially increasing record processing latency and reducing throughput. The default processing loop also skips punctuation and the commit stage for that iteration.

fields.description:
With {{{}group.protocol=streams{}}}, a new application instance can fail to join its group even when it uses the same logical topology, depending on the order in which source topics are supplied.

For example, two instances with the same {{application.id}} construct their topologies as follows:
 * Instance A joins {{stream(List.of("Aa", "BB"))}} with a stream from topic {{{}z{}}}.
 * Instance B joins {{stream(List.of("BB", "Aa"))}} with a stream from topic {{{}z{}}}.

All three topics have the same partition count. Node names, join settings, and all other configuration are identical. Only the source topic order differs, so both topologies have the same copartition constraints.

The client sorts the source topic list in the heartbeat, producing {{[Aa, BB, z]}} for both instances. However, copartition indexes are collected in Set iteration order, so A can send {{[0, 1, 2]}} while B sends {{{}[1, 0, 2]{}}}.

After A joins and its topology is stored, the coordinator treats B’s different index ordering as a topology change and returns:

 

{{INVALID_REQUEST: Topology updates are not supported yet.}}

B’s client treats this error as fatal, transitions from {{JOINING}} to {{{}FATAL{}}}, and stops sending heartbeats. As a result, adding or replacing an instance can fail despite the instances using logically identical topologies.

This occurs when the copartition list ordering actually differs. Reversing an arbitrary source topic list does not necessarily trigger the issue. In this example, {{Aa}} and {{BB}} have the same Java string hash code, allowing their input order to affect Set iteration order.
fields.summary: Streams group joins rejected due to copartition topic ordering differences

comments.body:
That doesn't sound like a minor bug. We should get it fixed.

Changed prio to criticial

Sorry, I didn't realize that this can only happen if the two topologies run different code (a.join(b) vs. b.join(a)). 

I think your initial judgement of "Minor" priority was correct
Ah, no problem at all!

Good point. So the bug triggers:
 * {{group.protocol=streams}} and a join, so the topology has a copartition group.
 * Those topics are subscribed by one source node through a collection with per-JVM iteration order (e.g. {{{}builder.stream(Set.of(...)){}}}), or members run equivalent but differently written topologies.
 * Two topics in that copartition group land in the same {{HashSet}} bucket (about 6% chance for a pair of topics).

That is more narrow than I originally thought, but it should definitely be fixed.

renderedFields.description:
With group.protocol=streams, a new application instance can fail to join its group even when it uses the same logical topology, depending on the order in which source topics are supplied.

For example, two instances with the same application.id construct their topologies as follows:

  • Instance A joins stream(List.of("Aa", "BB")) with a stream from topic z.
  • Instance B joins stream(List.of("BB", "Aa")) with a stream from topic z.

All three topics have the same partition count. Node names, join settings, and all other configuration are identical. Only the source topic order differs, so both topologies have the same copartition constraints.

The client sorts the source topic list in the heartbeat, producing [Aa, BB, z] for both instances. However, copartition indexes are collected in Set iteration order, so A can send [0, 1, 2] while B sends [1, 0, 2].

After A joins and its topology is stored, the coordinator treats B’s different index ordering as a topology change and returns:

 

INVALID_REQUEST: Topology updates are not supported yet.

B’s client treats this error as fatal, transitions from JOINING to FATAL, and stops sending heartbeats. As a result, adding or replacing an instance can fail despite the instances using logically identical topologies.

This occurs when the copartition list ordering actually differs. Reversing an arbitrary source topic list does not necessarily trigger the issue. In this example, Aa and BB have the same Java string hash code, allowing their input order to affect Set iteration order.

fields.description:
When a consumer group contains members using the classic protocol, reloading the group applies the consumer protocol session timeout to those members instead of their persisted session timeouts.

A classic member's session timeout is provided in its JoinGroup request and persisted in the member metadata. However, GroupMetadataManager.onLoaded() ignores this value and applies the consumer protocol session timeout to every member of the consumer group.

For example, if a classic member's session timeout is 10 seconds and the consumer protocol session timeout is 45 seconds, reloading the group after a coordinator change schedules the member's expiration for 45 seconds later. If the member sends no further heartbeats, failure detection and partition reassignment may be delayed.

Conversely, if the classic member's session timeout is 60 seconds and the consumer protocol session timeout is 45 seconds, the member may be removed before its configured timeout elapses if its next heartbeat has not yet arrived.

fields.summary: Streams group: a static member that rejoins from a new process can put a task on that process twice

renderedFields.description:
Problem

In a streams group (KIP-1071), one process must never hold the same task twice. CurrentAssignmentBuilder says "a single process must never run the same task twice". The reconciler enforces this only when it grants a task: the isUnreleased*Task checks run on tasks pending assignment, and a task the member already holds is kept without any check.

A static member that rejoins under a new member ID bypasses that check:

  1. The rejoin is accepted once the old member has left with epoch -2. GroupMetadataManager#getOrMaybeCreateStaticStreamsGroupMember copies the old member, including its assigned tasks.
  2. The heartbeat then sets the process ID from the request. Nothing compares it with the old process ID.
  3. If the rejoin comes from a different process, the copied tasks move to that process. If another member there already holds one of them as a standby or warm-up task, that process now holds the task twice.

The new target assignment that the process ID change triggers does not remove the duplicate. The sticky assignor keeps the active task on the rejoined member. The standby on the sibling member is revoked, but it stays until that member acknowledges the revocation.

When it happens

  • Kafka Streams with static membership: each stream thread uses group.instance.id "<id>-<threadIdx>". Member IDs are new on every restart, so a restarted thread always takes the rejoin path above.
  • The process ID changes across a restart when the topology has no persistent stores (StateDirectory#initializeProcessId creates a random UUID on every start), or when the state directory is lost or the instance moves to another host.
  • Sequence: an instance with two threads restarts under a new process ID B. Thread 2 rejoins first and is given the standby of task t, which is allowed because active t is still on the old process. Thread 1 rejoins and inherits active t. Process B now holds t both as an active task and as a standby task.

Impact

Both threads of the same instance are told to run t at the same time. This lasts until the next target assignment revokes the standby and the second thread acknowledges it: about one heartbeat interval, plus up to the assignment interval. From reading the client code:

  • With persistent stores, the task-directory lock makes the new active task retry until the standby releases it, so t stalls.
  • Without persistent stores, which is exactly the case where the process ID changes on every restart, the lock is a no-op. Both copies run, which duplicates memory and restore work.

Reproduction

The test below fails on trunk (dfd3dcab07) at the final assertion: process-B is both the active owner and a standby holder of s1_0.

package org.apache.kafka.coordinator.group;

import org.apache.kafka.common.Uuid;
import org.apache.kafka.common.message.StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequestData;
import org.apache.kafka.common.message.StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequestData.Subtopology;
import org.apache.kafka.common.message.StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequestData.TopicInfo;
import org.apache.kafka.common.message.StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequestData.Topology;
import org.apache.kafka.coordinator.common.runtime.CoordinatorMetadataImage;
import org.apache.kafka.coordinator.common.runtime.MetadataImageBuilder;
import org.apache.kafka.coordinator.group.streams.StreamsGroup;
import org.apache.kafka.coordinator.group.streams.StreamsGroupBuilder;
import org.apache.kafka.coordinator.group.streams.StreamsTopology;
import org.apache.kafka.coordinator.group.streams.TaskRole;
import org.apache.kafka.coordinator.group.streams.assignor.AssignmentConfigsImpl;
import org.apache.kafka.coordinator.group.streams.assignor.StickyTaskAssignor;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

import static org.apache.kafka.common.requests.StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequest.JOIN_GROUP_MEMBER_EPOCH;
import static org.apache.kafka.common.requests.StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequest.LEAVE_GROUP_STATIC_MEMBER_EPOCH;
import static org.apache.kafka.coordinator.group.StreamsGroupTestUtil.mkResponseTasks;
import static org.apache.kafka.coordinator.group.StreamsGroupTestUtil.streamsGroupMemberBuilderWithDefaults;
import static org.apache.kafka.coordinator.group.Utils.computeGroupHash;
import static org.apache.kafka.coordinator.group.Utils.computeTopicHash;
import static org.apache.kafka.coordinator.group.streams.TaskAssignmentTestUtil.mkTasks;
import static org.apache.kafka.coordinator.group.streams.TaskAssignmentTestUtil.mkTasksTuple;
import static org.apache.kafka.coordinator.group.streams.TaskAssignmentTestUtil.mkTasksTupleWithCommonEpoch;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertFalse;

class StreamsStaticRejoinProcessExclusivityTest {

    @Test
    public void staticRejoinFromNewProcessMustNotPutATaskOnAProcessTwice() {
        // One Kafka Streams instance with two stream threads (static instance IDs app-1 and app-2) ran on process A,
        // with num.standby.replicas=1 and a single stateful task s1_0. Thread app-1 ran the active task. Both threads
        // left with epoch -2, and the instance restarted under a new process ID B (no persistent stores, or a wiped
        // state directory), so each thread rejoins under a new member ID.
        Topology topology = new Topology().setSubtopologies(List.of(new Subtopology()
            .setSubtopologyId("s1")
            .setSourceTopics(List.of("in"))
            .setStateChangelogTopics(List.of(new TopicInfo().setName("store-changelog")))));
        CoordinatorMetadataImage image = new MetadataImageBuilder()
            .addTopic(Uuid.randomUuid(), "in", 1)
            .addTopic(Uuid.randomUuid(), "store-changelog", 1)
            .buildCoordinatorMetadataImage();
        GroupMetadataManagerTestContext context = new GroupMetadataManagerTestContext.Builder()
            .withStreamsGroupTaskAssignors(List.of(new StickyTaskAssignor()))
            .withMetadataImage(image)
            .withConfig(GroupCoordinatorConfig.STREAMS_GROUP_NUM_STANDBY_REPLICAS_CONFIG, 1)
            .withStreamsGroup(new StreamsGroupBuilder("app", 10)
                .withMember(streamsGroupMemberBuilderWithDefaults("t1-old", "app-1")
                    .setMemberEpoch(LEAVE_GROUP_STATIC_MEMBER_EPOCH)
                    .setPreviousMemberEpoch(10)
                    .setProcessId("process-A")
                    .setAssignedTasks(mkTasksTupleWithCommonEpoch(TaskRole.ACTIVE, 0, mkTasks("s1", 0)))
                    .build())
                .withMember(streamsGroupMemberBuilderWithDefaults("t2-old", "app-2")
                    .setMemberEpoch(LEAVE_GROUP_STATIC_MEMBER_EPOCH)
                    .setPreviousMemberEpoch(10)
                    .setProcessId("process-A")
                    .build())
                .withTargetAssignment("t1-old", mkTasksTuple(TaskRole.ACTIVE, mkTasks("s1", 0)))
                .withTargetAssignment("t2-old", mkTasksTuple(TaskRole.ACTIVE))
                .withTopology(StreamsTopology.fromHeartbeatRequest(topology))
                .withTargetAssignmentEpoch(10)
                .withMetadataHash(computeGroupHash(Map.of(
                    "in", computeTopicHash("in", image),
                    "store-changelog", computeTopicHash("store-changelog", image))))
                .withValidatedTopologyEpoch(0)
                .withLastAssignmentConfigs(new AssignmentConfigsImpl(1, List.of())))
            .build();
        StreamsGroup group = context.groupMetadataManager.streamsGroup("app");

        // Thread app-2 rejoins first. The active task is still on process A, so B may take the standby.
        var thread2 = context.streamsGroupHeartbeat(rejoin("t2-new", "app-2", "process-B", topology));
        assertEquals(mkResponseTasks("s1", 0), thread2.response().data().standbyTasks());

        // Thread app-1 rejoins right after. It inherits its old member's assignment, active s1_0, and moves it to
        // process B, where thread app-2 already holds the standby of s1_0.
        var thread1 = context.streamsGroupHeartbeat(rejoin("t1-new", "app-1", "process-B", topology));
        assertEquals(mkResponseTasks("s1", 0), thread1.response().data().activeTasks());

        // Fails today: process B now holds s1_0 both as an active task (t1-new) and as a standby task (t2-new).
        assertFalse(
            "process-B".equals(group.currentActiveTaskProcessId("s1", 0))
                && group.currentStandbyTaskProcessIds("s1", 0).contains("process-B"),
            "process-B holds task s1_0 as an active task and as a standby task at the same time");
    }

    private static StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequestData rejoin(String memberId, String instanceId, String processId,
                                                           Topology topology) {
        return new StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequestData()
            .setGroupId("app")
            .setMemberId(memberId)
            .setMemberEpoch(JOIN_GROUP_MEMBER_EPOCH)
            .setInstanceId(instanceId)
            .setProcessId(processId)
            .setRebalanceTimeoutMs(1500)
            .setTopology(topology)
            .setActiveTasks(List.of())
            .setStandbyTasks(List.of())
            .setWarmupTasks(List.of());
    }
}

Possible fix

When a static member rejoins from a different process, do not keep copied tasks that the new process already holds in another role. For example, the reconciler could put those tasks back in pending assignment, so the existing exclusivity checks apply to them.

fields.description:
{{StickyTaskAssignor#findPrevMemberWithLeastLoad}} picks one previous member by load, and the caller checks that member's quota only afterwards. If the picked member is at its quota, the lookup returns no member, even when another previous member of the task is below its quota. The task then goes to the least-loaded process, which may not have the task's state.

The candidate is replaced only when another member is strictly lower on both process load and member load, so a full member stays picked easily.

*Example:* task {{t}} has previous standby members {{a1}} (process A) and {{b1}} (process B), with {{a1}} first in the list.
 * {{a1}} is at the per-member quota. A's other member {{a2}} has no tasks, so A's process load is lower than B's.
 * {{b1}} is below the quota, but B's process load is not lower than A's, so {{a1}} stays picked.
 * The quota check on {{a1}} fails, and the standby of {{t}} goes to the least-loaded process (for example {{{}a2{}}}, which has no state), not to {{{}b1{}}}.

*Affected call sites:*
 * Active task assignment from previous standby members ({{{}hasUnfulfilledActiveTaskQuota{}}} checked after the lookup)
 * Standby task assignment from previous standby members ({{{}hasUnfulfilledTaskQuota{}}} checked after the lookup)
 * The rack-aware standby steps of KAFKA-20999, which use the same lookup

*Proposed fix:* check the quota inside {{{}findPrevMemberWithLeastLoad{}}}, skipping members that are at their quota, so the least-loaded previous member with room is picked. This changes some assignments, since more tasks stay on members that have their state.

StickyTaskAssignor#findPrevMemberWithLeastLoad picks one previous member by load, and the caller checks that member's quota only afterwards. If the picked member is at its quota, the lookup returns no member, even when another previous member of the task is below its quota. The task then goes to the least-loaded process, which may not have the task's state.

The candidate is replaced only when another member is strictly lower on both process load and member load, so a full member stays picked easily.

Example: task t has previous standby members a1 (process A) and b1 (process B), with a1 first in the list.

  • a1 is at the per-member quota. A's other member a2 has no tasks, so A's process load is lower than B's.
  • b1 is below the quota, but B's process load is not lower than A's, so a1 stays picked.
  • The quota check on a1 fails, and the standby of t goes to the least-loaded process (for example a2, which has no state), not to b1.

Affected call sites:

  • Active task assignment from previous standby members (hasUnfulfilledActiveTaskQuota checked after the lookup)
  • Standby task assignment from previous standby members (hasUnfulfilledTaskQuota checked after the lookup)
  • The rack-aware standby steps of KAFKA-20999, which use the same lookup

Proposed fix: check the quota inside findPrevMemberWithLeastLoad, skipping members that are at their quota, so the least-loaded previous member with room is picked. This changes some assignments, since more tasks stay on members that have their state.

fields.description:
A Java consumer on kafka-clients 4.1 or later, using {{group.protocol=consumer}} and {{{}subscribe(SubscriptionPattern){}}}, throws {{IllegalStateException("Use errorsByTopicId() when managing topic using topic id")}} when a topic assigned to it is deleted.
 * Since 4.1 (KAFKA-18117), this consumer asks for metadata by topic ID.
 * The broker answers a deleted topic's ID with {{UNKNOWN_TOPIC_ID}} and no name, which the schema allows from v12.
 * {{NetworkClient}} then reads the errors by topic name, and {{MetadataResponse.errors()}} throws on the row without a name.

As a consequence, the client never marks the Metadata request as finished, so it sends no more Metadata requests and never consumes new matching topics. This happens with default settings. With auto-commit disabled, we also saw it send {{ConsumerGroupHeartbeat}} continuously once a new matching topic was assigned.

kafka-clients 4.0.0 is not affected, nor are consumers subscribed by topic names. The code is unchanged on trunk.

Reproduce: [https://gist.github.com/jpalmerr/b653005afeb74d50346f8bf085d11ac5/ec78cbbbba3b10035858bd9d5f57e8e11effb36b]

The consumer logs this once, shortly after the delete:
{noformat}
ERROR Unexpected error caught in consumer network thread
java.lang.IllegalStateException: Use errorsByTopicId() when managing topic using topic id
at org.apache.kafka.common.requests.MetadataResponse.errors(MetadataResponse.java:99)
at org.apache.kafka.clients.NetworkClient$DefaultMetadataUpdater.handleSuccessfulResponse(NetworkClient.java:1293)
at org.apache.kafka.clients.NetworkClient.handleCompletedReceives(NetworkClient.java:1011)
at org.apache.kafka.clients.NetworkClient.poll(NetworkClient.java:654)
at org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.NetworkClientDelegate.poll(NetworkClientDelegate.java:166)
at org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.NetworkClientDelegate.poll(NetworkClientDelegate.java:148)
at org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.ConsumerNetworkThread.runOnce(ConsumerNetworkThread.java:228)
at org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.ConsumerNetworkThread.run(ConsumerNetworkThread.java:162)
{noformat}
A failing unit test in {{NetworkClientTest}} will follow as a PR. [edit:] pr https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23870

comments.body:
Thanks for reporting [~jpalmerrconduktor] , agree with the gap.

In case it helps, I see 2 sides to review here:
 # metadata response should handle the null name "gracefully", it's expected for requests that use topic IDs (re2j) if the topic was deleted (or unauthorized I expect, let's consider this case too) -> this is surely a gap to fix when we "handleMetadataResponse"
 # recovery: it's not happening but maybe this is just a cascading effect of 1? High level, I imagine the metadta path shouldn't break once we fix 1, and then it's the assignment path that will complete the recovery: the topic/partition should be eventually revoked when the GC realizes the topic was deleted, and the reconciliation will run even if the topic is not in metadata (the revoked set is computed based on the owned partition, the reconciliation client logic knows the names even if not in metadata)

Happy to help with reviews! Thanks, 

Lianet

Thanks [~lianetm]. 

I built the fix into the same branch. The pr should be ready for review now. 

James :)

Thanks for reporting jpalmerrconduktor , agree with the gap.

In case it helps, I see 2 sides to review here:

  1. metadata response should handle the null name "gracefully", it's expected for requests that use topic IDs (re2j) if the topic was deleted (or unauthorized I expect, let's consider this case too) -> this is surely a gap to fix when we "handleMetadataResponse"
