items.fromString:
A Java consumer on kafka-clients 4.1 or later, using \{{group.protocol=consumer}} and \{{subscribe(SubscriptionPattern)}}, throws \{{IllegalStateException("Use errorsByTopicId() when managing topic using topic id")}} when a topic assigned to it is deleted.

* Since 4.1 (KAFKA-18117), this consumer asks for metadata by topic ID.
* The broker answers a deleted topic's ID with \{{UNKNOWN_TOPIC_ID}} and no name, which the schema allows from v12.
* \{{NetworkClient}} then reads the errors by topic name, and \{{MetadataResponse.errors()}} throws on the row without a name.

As a consequence, the client never marks the Metadata request as finished, so it sends no more Metadata requests and never consumes new matching topics. This happens with default settings. With auto-commit disabled, we also saw it send \{{ConsumerGroupHeartbeat}} continuously once a new matching topic was assigned.

kafka-clients 4.0.0 is not affected, nor are consumers subscribed by topic names. The code is unchanged on trunk.

Reproduce: https://gist.github.com/jpalmerr/b653005afeb74d50346f8bf085d11ac5/ec78cbbbba3b10035858bd9d5f57e8e11effb36b

The consumer logs this once, shortly after the delete:

{noformat}
ERROR Unexpected error caught in consumer network thread
java.lang.IllegalStateException: Use errorsByTopicId() when managing topic using topic id
at org.apache.kafka.common.requests.MetadataResponse.errors(MetadataResponse.java:99)
at org.apache.kafka.clients.NetworkClient$DefaultMetadataUpdater.handleSuccessfulResponse(NetworkClient.java:1293)
at org.apache.kafka.clients.NetworkClient.handleCompletedReceives(NetworkClient.java:1011)
at org.apache.kafka.clients.NetworkClient.poll(NetworkClient.java:654)
at org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.NetworkClientDelegate.poll(NetworkClientDelegate.java:166)
at org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.NetworkClientDelegate.poll(NetworkClientDelegate.java:148)
at org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.ConsumerNetworkThread.runOnce(ConsumerNetworkThread.java:228)
at org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.ConsumerNetworkThread.run(ConsumerNetworkThread.java:162)
{noformat}

A failing unit test in \{{NetworkClientTest}} will follow as a PR.

fields.description:
KafkaFuture is one of the oldest and most commonly used classes in our public APIs. We introduced the method {{toCompletionStage}} to reduce the gap from the modern async style. It works, but it could be better. We assumed users would use {{toCompletionStage}} to chain the pipeline, but we missed the users who prefer the blocking style in lambdas. Unfortunately, the blocking method {{get}} has checked exceptions in its signature.

In short, this ticket introduces {{join}} to KafkaFuture. It could be a simple method with a default implementation, such as {{{}toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().join(){}}}.

fields.description:
In a couple of places, the coordinator runtime and group coordinator create and destroy tasks, eg. for regex resolution and (soon) asynchronous assignment calculations.

When coordinator state is rolled back, these tasks are not reverted and, when they complete, we have to think carefully about how we can discard their results if they no longer apply. It would be nice to have these tasks participate in the snapshot mechanism.

Analogous to KAFKA-19023 but for the CoordinatorExecutor.

fields.description:
Hello, I found this while prototyping key-based ordering for share groups. It reproduces on plain trunk.

A released batch stays AVAILABLE with an ongoing state transition, and keeps its acquisition lock, until the persister write completes.

So if the log start offset moves inside that batch in the meantime (retention or DeleteRecords removing records the group has not consumed yet, seen through an OFFSET_OUT_OF_RANGE fetch), archiveRecords splits it into per-offset states.

InFlightBatch.maybeInitializeOffsetStateUpdate() copies the batch lock to every offset, including the AVAILABLE ones, and the ongoing transition is not carried over, so the write completion never clears these locks.

The next acquire of one of these offsets moves it to ACQUIRED and then throws:
{code:java}
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Existing acquisition lock timeout exists, cannot override.
    at org.apache.kafka.server.share.fetch.InFlightState.updateAcquisitionLockTimeoutTask(InFlightState.java:107)
    at kafka.server.share.SharePartition.acquireSubsetBatchRecords(SharePartition.java:2047)
    at kafka.server.share.SharePartition.acquire(SharePartition.java:950){code}
The ShareFetch request fails with UNKNOWN_SERVER_ERROR, and the record stays ACQUIRED for a member that never received it until the stale lock expires. The timer task scheduled before the throw is left behind: in my runs it later released the record while another member was processing it.

The attached patch adds a test that reproduces it:SharePartitionTest#testReleasedRecordsSplitByLogStartOffsetMoveWhileReleaseWriteIsPendingCanBeAcquired.

Not splitting a batch that has an ongoing transition (or carrying the transition over), and not copying the lock to offsets that are not ACQUIRED, should fix it.

fields.description:
I found this while prototyping key-based ordering for share groups. It reproduces on plain trunk.

When a share partition is at share.partition.max.record.locks, lastOffsetAndMaxRecordsToAcquire caps lastOffsetToAcquire to the end offset. On a compacted topic, when the group lags enough for these records to be out of the active segment, the cleaner may remove the records between the fetch offset and the end offset, so the first fetched batch can start after the end offset, and acquire() calls cachedState.subMap(from, to) with from > to:
{code:java}
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: inconsistent range
    at java.base/java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentSkipListMap.subMap(ConcurrentSkipListMap.java:1912)
    at kafka.server.share.SharePartition.acquire(SharePartition.java:842){code}
In the simple case maybeArchiveStaleBatches has already archived the missing offsets, so one ShareFetch request fails with UNKNOWN_SERVER_ERROR and the partition recovers. After a re-initialization with a persister read gap at the start of the window, the gap window does not advance and every fetch at the gap start fails the same way (I checked 3 consecutive fetches).

The attached patch adds a test for the simple case:SharePartitionTest#testAcquireAtMaxInFlightRecordsWhenAvailableRecordsAreCompactedAway.

Returning an empty result when the first fetched batch starts after lastOffsetToAcquire, and moving the gap start past the compacted range, should fix it, I don't know if it creates other issues though, I let you decide how to solve this.

fields.description:
I found this while prototyping key-based ordering for share groups. It reproduces on plain trunk.

If an ACCEPT is being written to the persister when the log start offset moves past the acknowledged batch (retention or DeleteRecords catching up with a lagging group), archiveRecords leaves the batch alone because it is not AVAILABLE. If its acquisition lock then expires and the write fails, for example while the share coordinator is unavailable, completeStateTransition(false) moves the batch back to AVAILABLE, now below the start offset.

From then on nextFetchOffset() returns that offset, the fetch fails with OFFSET_OUT_OF_RANGE, and updateCacheAndOffsets() returns early because the log start offset is not greater than the start offset. Every fetch logs "The log start offset: 6 is not greater than the start offset: 6 ..." and returns no records, so the records after the start offset are never delivered. Only re-creating the SharePartition (leader change or broker restart) seems to recover it.

The attached patch adds a test that reproduces it:SharePartitionTest#testAcceptRolledBackAfterLockExpiryBelowMovedStartOffsetDoesNotStallFetches (nextFetchOffset() returns 0 instead of 6).

The lock timeout path already archives records below the start offset. Doing the same when a transition is rolled back with an expired lock should fix it, and nextFetchOffset() could also skip offsets below the start offset. I let you decide what is the best way to handle that though. 

 

Thanks

h3. Problem

{{PartitionStates}} keeps its order in a {{LinkedHashMap}} and moves a partition to the end with {{remove}} + {{put}} ({{updateAndMoveToEnd}}). {{HashMap.removeNode}} does not clear the {{next}} field of the removed entry (same in JDK 17, 21 and 25). When two partitions whose keys fall into the same bucket are updated in turn, every removed entry keeps pointing at the entry created after it, so the removed entries form one chain.

Once one entry of that chain is promoted to the old generation, every young GC treats the chain as live and copies all removed entries that follow it. The chain keeps growing as long as both partitions receive data. Because it is a linked list, a single GC worker copies it entry by entry, so pauses grow while the copied bytes stay small.

The only condition is two partitions that keep receiving data, fetched by the same fetcher thread, whose keys fall into the same bucket of that fetcher's map. The remove + put pattern has been there since KIP-74.

h3. Observed

Follower broker, Kafka 4.3.1, JDK 21, G1, 16 GiB heap, {{MaxGCPauseMillis=20}}:
* A mixed GC ran out of free regions ({{Survivor regions: 1->0(0)}}) and promoted the replica fetcher's map entries.
* Young GC pauses went from 11 ms to 34 ms on average (single pauses 30-50 ms) and stayed there until the broker was restarted. G1 then shrank Eden to keep up with the pause goal, which made young GCs about 6 times more frequent.
* A heap dump taken about 14 hours after the onset held 2,048,712 removed {{LinkedHashMap$Entry}} objects linked through {{next}}, alternating between the two partitions of one bucket of one fetcher's map.

Reproduction without a broker: updating two such partitions in turn one million times leaves 2,000,002 entries reachable from the first removed entry.

h3. Fix

Pull request: https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23839

Keep the order in a doubly linked list of nodes looked up through a {{HashMap}}, and move the existing node to the end instead of creating a new one. This matches what the leader side already does for fetch sessions with {{ImplicitLinkedHashCollection}}. {{LinkedHashMap.putLast}} would do the same in one call but needs Java 21, and the clients module still targets Java 11.

Order, {{partitionStateMap()}} (a live unmodifiable view) and {{size()}} behave as before. {{stateIterator().remove()}} is no longer supported; no caller uses it, and with the old code it left {{size()}} stale.

A new JMH benchmark ({{PartitionStatesBenchmark}}, JDK 21) shows {{updateAndMoveToEnd}} going from 11.6-13.3 ns and 40 B/op to 5.5-8.6 ns and 0 B/op. {{ReplicaFetcherThreadBenchmark}} is faster at 100-1000 partitions and within the error at 5000.
fields.summary: Removed entries in PartitionStates stay chained and slow down young GC on follower brokers

comments.body:
h3. Additional test results

h4. Reproduction on test clusters

Setup: three test clusters (follower heap 1 GiB, 2 GiB and 6 GiB, G1, JDK 21). Two topics were picked so that their partitions are fetched by the same fetcher thread (abs(31 * topic.hashCode() + partition) % num.replica.fetchers) and land in the same bucket of that fetcher's map. Consecutive partitions of one topic rarely share a bucket, so this needs to be computed. Each partition of the pair received about 1,000 records/s.

Measurement: trigger a full GC on the follower so that live entries are promoted, wait 10 minutes, take a heap dump, and count the longest chain of removed LinkedHashMap$Entry objects linked through next.

||Heap||Original PartitionStates (runs)||With the fix (runs)||
|1 GiB|339,594 / 5,855 / 8,256 / 838|2 / 2 / 3 / 2|
|2 GiB|7,713 / 309,597|3 / 3|
|6 GiB|2,820 / 2,868|4 / 4|

The original code reproduced the chain in every run; one promotion is enough, whatever causes it. With the fix the longest chain stayed at 2-4 in every run, which is just the garbage between two young GCs. As a control, the original code without a same-bucket pair gave 34.

h4. When it gets bad

The cluster where we hit it has many partitions with small, continuous writes, so followers fetch very often (about 4,500 follower fetches/s per broker) and the chain grows quickly. On that 18-broker cluster, 7 brokers had at least one same-bucket pair with continuous writes. Removed entries are only created when a fetch returns data (validBytes > 0), so idle partitions do not contribute.

h4. Regression testing

* clients unit tests (13,134), consumer integration tests (375) and core kafka.server.* tests (1,998) on 4.3.1 with the patch. Two failures (KafkaProducerTest.negativePartitionShouldThrow, PlaintextConsumerTest.testAsyncConsumerEndOffsets) passed when re-run three times each; the second also passes on the original code.
* Our end-to-end suite on a 3-broker cluster passed: produce/consume, broker restart, broker kill, controller restart, quota throttling, authentication paths, broker failure, in-place upgrade and scale-out.

h4. Production

The patch has been running in production on the cluster where we hit the issue (18 brokers, 16 GiB heap) since October 19, with no recurrence. The slowdown used to start about 7.5 hours after a restart; since the rollout no broker has gone above 15 ms average young GC pause in any hour, including today under about 1 GiB/s of new inbound traffic and 4-6 GiB/s outbound.

||Metric||Same 19-hour window, day before||After the rollout||
|Young GC time (18 brokers, per hour)|49.5 s|22.1 s|
|Highest per-broker 1-hour average young GC pause|35.8 ms|12.1 ms|
|Survivor regions dropping to 0 / full GC|-|0 / 0|

The same rollout also included an unrelated change that reduced heap pressure from large buffers in a tiered storage plugin, so these production numbers are for both changes together; the test runs above isolate this patch.

fields.description:
UnifiedLog.searchOffsetInLocalLog returns immediately from the first segment whose largestTimestamp meets the requested timestamp, even when that segment's findOffsetByTimestamp returns empty.

This can incorrectly return no result for a timestamp lookup when the log start offset has advanced into a segment and a later segment contains a valid match.

*Reproduction*
Confirmed on Apache Kafka trunk commit:
8e46092edac3e837972ee13b40dcc149e7113ae7
(4.5.0-SNAPSHOT, tested October 20, 2026)

1. Append offset 0 at timestamp T and offset 1 at timestamp T-1 into the first segment.
2. Roll the log and append offset 2 at timestamp T into the second segment.
3. Advance the high watermark to the log end.
4. Advance the log start offset to 1, as with DeleteRecords, leaving the first segment physically present.
5. Query timestamp T.

Expected: timestamp T at offset 2.
Actual: an empty result.

*Root cause*
The first segment remains eligible because its cached largest timestamp comes from offset 0. LogSegment correctly excludes that record because it is below the log start offset. UnifiedLog then returns the empty result without searching the second segment.

*Proposed fix*
Continue searching eligible segments until a lookup returns a result. Use in-memory segment base offsets to skip obsolete segments without reading segment tails.

*Validation*
- The new regression fails with trunk production code unchanged.
- The same regression passes with the fix applied.
- All 243 tests in UnifiedLogTest and LogSegmentTest pass.
- Storage Spotless, Checkstyle, and SpotBugs checks pass.

*Proposed patch:*
https://github.com/shantanukawale-stripe/kafka/tree/fix-unified-log-timestamp-search

Related issues
KAFKA-10875 reports similar symptoms, but equivalence has not been established.
KAFKA-21204 concerns the upper fetchable offset bound, not this cross-segment search failure.

fields.description:
In the group coordinator, we maintain `invertedTargetAssignment` for each group as a map of partitions to owning member ids. Then in the assignor `GroupSpec`, we use it to answer `isPartitionAssigned` queries.

Share groups can assign the same partition to multiple members, which breaks tracking of `invertedTargetAssignment`. eg. When a share group member leaves, its assigned partitions can be cleared in `invertedTargetAssignment` and then `isPartitionAssigned` will return `false` for those partitions even when other members still have them assigned.

fields.description:
I found this while prototyping key-based ordering for share groups. It reproduces on plain trunk.

With share.isolation.level=read_committed, filterAbortedTransactionalAcquiredRecords looks up each aborted batch of the fetched data with cachedState.floorEntry(batch.baseOffset()). If the share partition start offset lies inside an aborted batch, for example after DeleteRecords to a mid-batch offset or, from reading the code, when a by_duration auto offset reset lands there, the cached batch starts at the start offset, so nothing in the cache starts at or below the aborted batch base offset, and fetchSubMap throws after the records were acquired:


{code:java}
java.lang.IllegalStateException: Batch record not found. The request batch offsets are not found in the cache.
    at kafka.server.share.SharePartition.fetchSubMap(SharePartition.java:3309)
    at kafka.server.share.SharePartition.filterAbortedTransactionalAcquiredRecords(SharePartition.java:3207)
    at kafka.server.share.SharePartition.acquire(SharePartition.java:861){code}

The fetched records stay ACQUIRED and are not delivered, and each retry after the lock expires fails the same way and uses a delivery attempt.

With share.delivery.count.limit=2, the committed records after the aborted batch are archived without ever being delivered. With the default limit of 5, the committed records are delivered in the end, after 7 failed fetches, once delivery throttling has archived the aborted records one by one. 

The attached patch adds a test that reproduces it: SharePartitionTest#testAcquireReadCommittedWhenStartOffsetIsWithinAbortedTransactionBatch.

Looking up max(batch.baseOffset(), startOffset) instead of batch.baseOffset(), or skipping aborted batches that do not overlap the cached range, should fix it.

fields.summary: Streams group: the assignment refiner does not see a member that joins in the same heartbeat

renderedFields.description:
Problem

When a streams group heartbeat computes a new target assignment, GroupMetadataManager#refineAssignment passes group.members() to the refiner (GroupMetadataManager:4707). That map does not contain the member sending the heartbeat yet, because the heartbeat's records are replayed only after the handler returns. The target assignment the refiner gets, however, comes from UpdatedMembersAndTargetAssignmentView, which already adds that member, or relabels a replaced static member to its new member ID (:4583-4595).

So the refiner treats a target owner that joins in this heartbeat as a member that has left the group, and its result is cached as the epoch's intermediate assignment.

Effects

With warm-up tasks enabled (the default), for stateful tasks:

  1. A static member that rejoins under a new member ID gets none of its tasks when the same heartbeat computes a new target, for example because it rejoins from a new process. The refiner keeps its active tasks on the old member ID, which the replacement removes. The member is told nothing, and no member runs those tasks until the next refinement step.
  2. A new member gets no warm-up task. A stateful task the target moves to it stays on its old owner without a warm-up, even when warm-up slots are free, until the next refinement step.
  3. A task can run num.standby.replicas + 1 standbys. If the new member is the target standby holder of a task whose migration borrows an existing standby, its standby is not held back (AssignmentRefinerImpl:866-872, :818-823). Once delivered it is kept, so the extra standby lasts until the migration completes.

The refiner's branches for a target owner missing from members (AssignmentRefinerImpl:286-293) attribute that case to assignment offloading and member fencing. Neither produces it on trunk: streams assignor offloading is not wired up, and fencing removes the member's target assignment together with the member. So today these branches fire only for a member that joins in the same heartbeat.

Possible fix

Pass the view's members to the refiner, together with the view's target assignment.

Reproduction

The test below fails on trunk (46dc4b51f7) with expected: <[TaskIds(subtopologyId='s1', partitions=[0])]> but was: <[]>. Place it in group-coordinator/src/test/java/org/apache/kafka/coordinator/group/. Effects 2 and 3 reproduce the same way, with a joining dynamic member.

            .withStreamsGroupTaskAssignors(List.of(assignor))
            .withStreamsGroupAssignmentRefiner(new AssignmentRefinerImpl())
            .withMetadataImage(image)
            .withStreamsGroup(new StreamsGroupBuilder("app", 10)
                .withMember(streamsGroupMemberBuilderWithDefaults("member-old", "instance-1")
                    .setMemberEpoch(LEAVE_GROUP_STATIC_MEMBER_EPOCH)
                    .setPreviousMemberEpoch(10)
                    .setProcessId("process-A")
                    .setAssignedTasks(mkTasksTupleWithCommonEpoch(TaskRole.ACTIVE, 10, mkTasks("s1", 0)))

                .withTopology(StreamsTopology.fromHeartbeatRequest(topology))
                .withValidatedTopologyEpoch(0)
                .withMetadataHash(computeGroupHash(Map.of(
                    "in", computeTopicHash("in", image),

                .withLastAssignmentConfigs(AssignmentConfigsImpl.DEFAULT))
            .build();

        // It rejoins under a new member ID from process B. The process change bumps the group epoch, so the target
        // assignment is computed and refined in this heartbeat.
        CoordinatorResult<StreamsGroupHeartbeatResult, CoordinatorRecord> result = context.streamsGroupHeartbeat(
            new StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequestData()
                .setGroupId("app")
                .setMemberId("member-new")
                .setMemberEpoch(JOIN_GROUP_MEMBER_EPOCH)
                .setInstanceId("instance-1")
                .setProcessId("process-B")

                .setActiveTasks(List.of())
                .setStandbyTasks(List.of())
                .setWarmupTasks(List.of()));

        // s1_0 on member-old, which the replacement removes. member-new is told nothing, and no member runs s1_0.
        assertEquals(mkResponseTasks("s1", 0), result.response().data().activeTasks());
    }

renderedFields.description:
streams/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/streams/query/WindowKeyQuery.java has the wrong parameter order in the private ctor. The builder method withKeyAndWindowStartRange invokes the constructor with

new WindowKeyQuery<>(key, Optional.of(timeFrom), Optional.of(timeTo))

while the order is

private WindowKeyQuery(final K key, final Optional<Instant> timeTo, final Optional<Instant> timeFrom)

The actual order should be

private WindowKeyQuery(final K key, final Optional<Instant> timeFrom, final Optional<Instant> timeTo)

While this has been noticed and fixed on the trunk (included in 4.4.0 release) branch as part of KAKFA-20705, there is no dedicated issue nor it's fixed in already released Kafka versions.

Could we backport this, at least for Kafka 4.x? I'd be willing to submit a PR.

fields.description:
KIP-909 (KAFKA-14648) added {{{}bootstrap.resolve.timeout.ms{}}}, which lets clients
resolve bootstrap DNS asynchronously instead of blocking at construction. It
currently defaults to {{0}} (synchronous, original behavior), and KAFKA-20939
forces it off entirely in Connect and Streams after issues surfaced during
early adoption. As a result the feature has stayed opt-in rather than becoming
the default.

This ticket tracks the work needed to responsibly enable it by default:
 * Close remaining test coverage gaps around the async resolution path
  (retry/recovery behavior, and shutdown while a resolution is in flight).
 * Decide on and implement proper support in Connect and Streams, which
  currently disable the feature outright.
 * Re-evaluate the default value of {{bootstrap.resolve.timeout.ms}} once the
  above are addressed.

This is an umbrella/tracking ticket, work will happen in linked sub-tasks.

fields.summary: Enable Gradle configuration cache

comments.body:
I tried to figure out would it be possible to disable configuration cache in Gradle 10 and it seems that priorities are changed: Gradle will push enablement-by-a-default for this feature to Gradle 11:
 * [https://adtmag.com/articles/2026/08/27/gradle-shifts-build-tool-priorities-as-ai-coding-agents-become-users.aspx]
 * [https://blog.gradle.org/gradle-is-going-agentic]  
{quote}*We're making Gradle work well with coding agents, and that meant not shipping Configuration Cache by default in Gradle 10 this cycle.*
{quote}

This probably means that configuration cache will not be mandatory for a quite a long time (probably not even in Gradle 11) and hence issue link to KAFKA-20102 is changed from _*blocks*_ to _*relates to*_
 
*However: configuration cache is the preferred mode of execution since Gradle 9.0.0:*
* [https://blog.gradle.org/road-to-configuration-cache#preferred-mode-of-execution]
* [https://docs.gradle.org/9.7.1/userguide/best_practices_performance.html#use_configuration_cache]

so it makes sense to push forward with this ticket.

fields.description:
Kafka's documentation under {{docs/}} (Hugo source for kafka-site) contains hardcoded version references in structured contexts:
 * Maven {{<version>}} coordinates,
 * Docker image tags ({{{}apache/kafka:X.Y.Z{}}}),
 * tarball/jar names ({{{}kafka_2.13-X.Y.Z.tgz{}}}, {{{}connect-file-X.Y.Z.jar{}}}),
 * GitHub source links ({{{}blob/X.Y/...{}}}),
 * archetype versions ({{{}-DarchetypeVersion=X.Y.Z{}}}),
 * andjavadoc link titles ("Kafka X.Y Javadoc").

When a doc page is created by copy-pasting from an existing page (very common), these version strings are frequently carried over unchanged and never updated.

They then silently go stale until someone notices during a release — e.g. the 4.4 docs still referenced 4.3 in numerous places, caught only by manual review during release staging.

I would like to propose an automated guard against this to prevent stale references accumulate across a release cycle and land on the release manager at staging time — the worst place to triage them, since the RM lacks the context for every line written months earlier by other contributors.

*Proposal:*

Add a CI check (new workflow + script under {{{}.github/scripts/{}}}) that runs on any PR touching {{{}docs/**{}}}, including on trunk (trunk is where most stale references are first introduced).

The check asserts that a small set of *high-signal, structured* version patterns resolve to the current version (derived from {{{}gradle.properties{}}}), and flags any that point at a different, non-{{{}trunk{}}} version:
 *  {{<version>X.Y.Z</version>}} and the sbt {{% "X.Y.Z"}} form
 * {{{}apache/kafka:X.Y.Z{}}}, {Unknown macro: \{apache/kafka-native}}
 * {{kafka_2.13-X.Y.Z.tgz}} / {Unknown macro: \{kafka_2.13-X.Y.Z}}
 * {{{}connect-file-X.Y.Z.jar{}}}, {Unknown macro: \{kafka-storage-X.Y.Z-test.jar}}

 * 
Unknown macro: \{{-DarchetypeVersion=X.Y.Z}}
 * {{blob/X.Y/}} (allowing {{{}blob/trunk/{}}})
 * "Kafka X.Y Javadoc"
 * {\\{git checkout X.Y.Z}}

items.toString:
Kafka's documentation under {{docs/}} (Hugo source for kafka-site) contains hardcoded version references in structured contexts:
 * Maven {{<version>}} coordinates,
 * Docker image tags ({{{}apache/kafka:X.Y.Z{}}}),
 * tarball/jar names ({{{}kafka_2.13-X.Y.Z.tgz{}}}, {{{}connect-file-X.Y.Z.jar{}}}),
 * GitHub source links ({{{}blob/X.Y/...{}}}),
 * archetype versions ({{{}-DarchetypeVersion=X.Y.Z{}}}),
 * andjavadoc link titles ("Kafka X.Y Javadoc").

When a doc page is created by copy-pasting from an existing page (very common), these version strings are frequently carried over unchanged and never updated.

They then silently go stale until someone notices during a release — e.g. the 4.4 docs still referenced 4.3 in numerous places, caught only by manual review during release staging.

I would like to propose an automated guard against this to prevent stale references accumulate across a release cycle and land on the release manager at staging time — the worst place to triage them, since the RM lacks the context for every line written months earlier by other contributors.

*Proposal:*

Add a CI check (new workflow + script under {{{}.github/scripts/{}}}) that runs on any PR touching {{{}docs/**{}}}, including on trunk (trunk is where most stale references are first introduced).

The check asserts that a small set of *high-signal, structured* version patterns resolve to the current version (derived from {{{}gradle.properties{}}}), and flags any that point at a different, non-{{{}trunk{}}} version:
 *  {{<version>X.Y.Z</version>}} and the sbt {{% "X.Y.Z"}} form
 * {{{}apache/kafka:X.Y.Z{}}}, {Unknown macro: \{apache/kafka-native}}
 * {{kafka_2.13-X.Y.Z.tgz}} / {Unknown macro: \{kafka_2.13-X.Y.Z}}
 * {{{}connect-file-X.Y.Z.jar{}}}, {Unknown macro: \{kafka-storage-X.Y.Z-test.jar}}

 * 
Unknown macro: \{{-DarchetypeVersion=X.Y.Z}}
 * {{blob/X.Y/}} (allowing {{{}blob/trunk/{}}})
 * "Kafka X.Y Javadoc"
 * {\\{git checkout X.Y.Z}}

fields.description:
In Kafka Streams the InternalTopicManager retries internal topic
describe/create/validate on a fixed \{{retry.backoff.ms}} (default 100 ms) until
{\{max.poll.interval.ms}} / 2 (default 150 s). The backoff never grows and has no jitter. During a
broker outage that is up to ~1,500 retry rounds per application, and applications on the same
cluster that rebalance after the same outage retry in lockstep.

The producer, consumer and admin clients already back off exponentially with jitter (KIP-580,
{\{org.apache.kafka.common.utils.ExponentialBackoff}}). InternalTopicManager should do the same.

Out of scope: the streams rebalance protocol (KIP-1071), where the broker creates internal topics.

Depends on KAFKA-21033 (https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23363), which moves the backoff back
to one sleep per round in maybeSleep and switches it to time.sleep. This change should build on
that.

fields.description:
When a TLS close_notify arrives in the same socket read as application data, SslTransportLayer.read() returns the data and leaves the close to be handled by a later read. However, updateBytesBuffered() clears hasBytesBuffered once the buffers are empty, so the Selector only reads the channel again if the socket becomes readable, which requires a TCP FIN.

RFC 8446 section 6.1 allows a peer to send close_notify and keep the TCP connection open: close_notify closes only the sender's write side, and the standard leaves the transport lifecycle to the application. A TLS-terminating proxy that half-closes its TLS side (for example, Envoy's tcp_proxy) does exactly this. The client then never notices the disconnect, and an in-flight request waits for request.timeout.ms before it fails.

*Reproduction*
A TLS peer completes the handshake, then writes part (or all) of a response followed by close_notify in a single write, and keeps the TCP connection open. The client Selector never reports the connection as disconnected. If the full response was sent, the client receives it but still does not see the disconnect.

*Expected behaviour*
Kafka already treats close_notify as end-of-stream when it arrives on its own: the CLOSED unwrap makes read() throw EOFException and the channel is closed. It should do the same when close_notify arrives together with data. This matches RFC 8446 section 6.1, which requires a TLS implementation to receive close_notify before indicating end-of-data to the application, and does not require the receiver to keep its own write side open. Kafka has no half-close semantics: once the peer has sent close_notify it can send no more responses, so reporting the disconnect at once is the only useful behaviour. On close, SslTransportLayer still sends its own close_notify.

*Proposed fix*
* After a CLOSED unwrap, keep the channel in the Selector's buffered-read set (hasBytesBuffered = true) so the next poll() reads it again without waiting for OP_READ.
* At the start of read(), if the engine's inbound side is done and no decrypted data is left, throw EOFException so the channel is closed as a disconnect.
* In read(ByteBuffer[], int, int), return the bytes already read if a later read throws EOFException, instead of losing them.

A channel that is muted (for example while the broker handles a request that arrived with the close_notify) stays open until it is unmuted, so the response to that request is still sent before the disconnect is reported.

fields.description:
Bootstrap DNS resolution currently calls InetAddress/InetSocketAddress directly, bypassing HostResolver, the abstraction NetworkClient already uses elsewhere to make DNS behavior injectable in tests.

This is why the async bootstrap path is hard to test today. Proposed change: route bootstrap resolution through HostResolver too, using the same injection point already exposed by KafkaAdminClient. A local prototype confirms this works, compiles cleanly, and passes the existing test suite. This unblocks writing recovery/retry test coverage for the async bootstrap path.

fields.description:
Today, {{release.py}} dispatches on three subcommands only: the default {{{}stage{}}}, {{{}stage-docs{}}}, and {{{}release-email{}}}. There is no {{blog}} subcommand. The tooling automates two emails during a release — the RC vote email and the release announcement email ({{{}release/templates.py{}}}: {{{}rc_vote_email_text{}}}, {{{}release_announcement_email{}}}) — but the actual release announcement {*}blog post{*}(e.g. {{{}kafka-site/content/en/blog/releases/ak-X.Y.Z.md{}}}) along side `downloads.md` is still written entirely by hand by the release manager for every release.

In practice, the release manager has to manually:
 # Create the blog post file with the correct frontmatter (date, title, slug, author).
 # Re-derive and restate upgrade notes, notable changes, and KIPs in release plan
 # Cross-check version numbers, links, and contributor mentions by hand.

This is repetitive, error-prone (version/date typos, missed KIPs), and slows down the release-week checklist.

 

*Proposal:*

Add a command (e.g. {{{}./release.py blog{}}}) that writes a skeleton {{ak-XYZ.md}} with:
 * Hugo front matter populated (title, date, author/RM, any required taxonomy fields)
 * The standard section headings, in the standard order
 * Version strings and the release date substituted everywhere they appear
 * The contributor acknowledgement list, generated via the existing git helper in {{{}release/{}}}, deduped and sorted

 * A {{<!-- TODO -->}} marker in each body slot the RM must write
 * The `downloads.md` section populated with the full set of artifact/checksum/signature links for the version.

fields.description:
When a broker becomes the leader of a {{__transaction_state}} partition, {{TransactionStateManager.loadTransactionMetadata}} reads the log up to the log end offset ({{FetchIsolation.LOG_END}}). A newly elected leader can have records above the high watermark: they were replicated to it but not yet committed. These records can still be truncated if leadership moves again before they are committed. This can happen even with clean elections: another ISR member that doesn't have them can be elected.

Then the coordinator acts on state that is later rolled back. The most damaging case is a PREPARE_COMMIT or PREPARE_ABORT above the high watermark. After the load, the coordinator sends the markers for it right away. For example:

# The coordinator appends PREPARE_COMMIT for a transaction. The record reaches follower B but not follower C, and the leader fails before the high watermark advances.
# B becomes the leader and loads the partition, including the uncommitted PREPARE_COMMIT. It starts sending COMMIT markers, and some data partitions commit.
# B fails before C replicates the record. C, which is in the ISR, becomes the leader, and the PREPARE_COMMIT is gone. C loads the transaction as ONGOING.
# The transaction times out, and C aborts it: PREPARE_ABORT, then ABORT markers to the remaining partitions.

The transaction ends up committed on some partitions and aborted on others.

Smaller effects of acting on state that is later truncated: client responses or fencing decisions based on state that disappears, and producer epochs being reused after the rollback.

Since the coordinator only updates its in-memory state after an append with acks=all completes, only the last transition of each transactional id can be uncommitted. So the rollback is at most one step per transactional id.

Using {{FetchIsolation.HIGH_WATERMARK}} for the load is not enough. A newly elected leader's high watermark can lag behind the true one, so the load would miss committed records. For example, it could miss a committed PREPARE_COMMIT and then abort the transaction on timeout.

Proposed fix:

The coordinator doesn't write to the partition while it is loading: requests get COORDINATOR_LOAD_IN_PROGRESS. So the log end offset at the start of the load doesn't change. Once the high watermark reaches it, every record the load reads is committed. A new leader's high watermark only advances after the ISR followers fetch from it (their logs are prefixes of the leader's log after truncation). In the normal case, the wait is about one follower fetch round trip.

* In {{loadTransactionsForTxnTopicPartition}}, if the high watermark is below the log end offset, register a {{PartitionListener}} ({{ReplicaManager.maybeAddListener}}). Schedule the load once {{onHighWatermarkUpdated}} reports an offset at or above the log end offset recorded when the wait started.
* Check the high watermark again after registering. {{Partition.maybeAddListener}} replays the current state before it adds the listener, and high watermark updates from follower fetches can happen between the replay and the insertion.
* If the leader epoch changes, the partition becomes a follower, or it fails or is deleted before the high watermark catches up, abandon the load: remove the epoch's {{loadingPartitions}} entry. Do this on the load scheduler, since the listener is invoked with partition locks held.
* {{removeExpiredTransactionalIds()}} should skip partitions that are loading. On a leader epoch bump, the previous epoch's cache entry stays until the new load replaces it. Expiration can write tombstones for it, which would move the log end offset while the load waits.

fields.description:
{{max.poll.records}} and {{max.poll.interval.ms}} are read when a consumer is constructed and neither can be changed afterwards.

If processing slows down, a batch that used to fit inside the poll interval stops fitting. The consumer misses its deadline and leaves the group. The assignment is released through {{{}onPartitionsLost{}}}, so the in-flight batch was never committed and the next owner reprocesses it.

The consumer rejoins and asks for the same batch size without any changes to config. It misses the deadline again. This continues until the slowdown ends. A shared dependency degrades for all members at once, so they hit it together and the group rebalances repeatedly. The common response is a process restart after increasing {{max.poll.interval.ms}} or decreasing {{{}max.poll.records{}}}, which reassigns every group in that JVM.



We can consider providing an API to lower the records from each poll operation to fit the best batch size that the client can currently deliver
fields.summary: Per-call record limit for Consumer poll

renderedFields.description:
max.poll.records and max.poll.interval.ms are read when a consumer is constructed and neither can be changed afterwards.

If processing slows down, a batch that used to fit inside the poll interval stops fitting. The consumer misses its deadline and leaves the group. The assignment is released through onPartitionsLost, so the in-flight batch was never committed and the next owner reprocesses it.

The consumer rejoins and asks for the same batch size without any changes to config. It misses the deadline again. This continues until the slowdown ends. A shared dependency degrades for all members at once, so they hit it together and the group rebalances repeatedly. The common response is a process restart after increasing max.poll.interval.ms or decreasing max.poll.records, which reassigns every group in that JVM.

We can consider providing an API to lower the records from each poll operation to fit the best batch size that the client can currently deliver

fields.description:
The success message printed by kafka-metadata-quorum.sh remove-controller contains two spaces before "KRaft".

Actual output:

Removed  KRaft controller 2003 with directory id MkWfVYpS_qAWFaz7GuOkRg

The dry-run output has the same issue:

DRY RUN of removing  KRaft controller 2003 with directory id MkWfVYpS_qAWFaz7GuOkRg

Expected output:

Removed KRaft controller 2003 with directory id MkWfVYpS_qAWFaz7GuOkRg

DRY RUN of removing KRaft controller 2003 with directory id MkWfVYpS_qAWFaz7GuOkRg

Cause:

The value supplied for %s already ends with a space, while the format string adds another space after %s:

System.out.printf("%s KRaft controller %d with directory id %s%n",
    dryRun ? "DRY RUN of removing " : "Removed ",
    controllerId,
    directoryId);

Suggested change:

System.out.printf("%sKRaft controller %d with directory id %s%n",
    dryRun ? "DRY RUN of removing " : "Removed ",
    controllerId,
    directoryId);

The corresponding unit-test expectation should also be changed to use one space.

This issue affects Apache Kafka 3.9.x through 4.3.x. It is already corrected in 4.4.0 and trunk as part of KAFKA-20395 / PR #22191, but the correction has not been backported to the affected release branches.

There is no functional impact; this only corrects the CLI output formatting.

fields.description:
Enabling DLQ on a share group record could strangulate the overall share fetch throughput by choking the persister. The causes are (in order of priority):
1. `ShareCoordinatorMetadataCacheHelperImpl.isDlqEnabledOnTopic` returns the value of a dynamic config so it is called repeatedly. The impl of this method creates a new LogConfig object, on each invocation and parses entire TopicConfig. On a system with large number of DLQ requests, these calls add up consuming CPU and choking the persister.
Fix: Use raw config lookup (shrinks cpu samples at high load from 27% to 0.1%)

2. Extra batch reads in `ShareGroupDLQRecordFetcher.collectRecords` - each DLQ request reads from the source log with maxFetchBytes of 1 MiB, which is about X batches of Y KB (for example 64 batches of 16KB). The loop in collectRecords stops only when shouldStop() said the size budget was used up. Currently, we are looking at all these batches instead of stopping when we have records for DLQ'ed offsets.
Fix: Discard batches by looking at baseOffset

3. Share group DLQ requires reading data from the ReplicaManagerLogReader, which is a disk operation. Currently, this happens in the same thread as the Persister which means that other share coordinator requests remain queued on a potentially slow disk read operation, again choking the persister.
Fix: Allocate separate executor to the record readers.

fields.description:
h3. Problem

When {{topology.optimization=all}} is set, {{StreamsBuilder.build()}} throws this exception {*}for a topology with nested merges{*}:
{noformat}
org.apache.kafka.streams.errors.StreamsException: Found a null keyChangingChild node for OptimizableRepartitionNode{ BaseRepartitionNode{... repartitionTopic='grp-repartition', ...} StreamsGraphNode{nodeName='grp-repartition-source', ..., parentNodes=[]} }
{noformat}
The failure occurs when all of these conditions are true:
 # A key-changing operation feeds a merge (the inner merge).
 # The inner merge feeds a second merge (the outer merge).
 # An optimizable repartition (for example {{{}groupByKey().count(){}}}) follows the outer merge.
 # No other key-changing operation sits between them.

The same topology builds without an error on 4.2.2 and earlier.
h3. Reproduction
{code:java}
StreamsBuilder b = new StreamsBuilder();
KStream<String, String> f1 = b.<String, String>stream("a").selectKey((k, v) -> v);
KStream<String, String> f2 = b.<String, String>stream("b").selectKey((k, v) -> v);
KStream<String, String> j  = b.<String, String>stream("c").selectKey((k, v) -> v);

f1.merge(f2).merge(j)
  .groupByKey(Grouped.with("grp", Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()))
  .count();

Properties p = new Properties();
p.put(StreamsConfig.APPLICATION_ID_CONFIG, "repro");
p.put(StreamsConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "localhost:9092");
p.put(StreamsConfig.TOPOLOGY_OPTIMIZATION_CONFIG, StreamsConfig.OPTIMIZE);
b.build(p); // throws on 4.3.x and 4.4.0
{code}
||Version||Result||
|4.1.2|OK|
|4.2.2|OK|
|4.3.1|StreamsException|
|4.4.0|StreamsException|

A single merge with three inputs (a merge node with three parents) builds without an error on 4.4.0.
h3. Cause

KAFKA-20264 changed {{{}InternalStreamsBuilder.findParentNodeMatching{}}}. The method now returns the first match in a depth-first search. Before the change, it returned the result of the last parent. The change is correct, but it exposes a defect in {{{}maybeUpdateKeyChangingRepartitionNodeMap{}}}.

In the reproduction, M1 = {{{}f1.merge(f2){}}}, M2 = {{{}M1.merge(j){}}}, and R is the repartition node below M2.
 # {{getKeyChangingParentNode(R)}} searches up through M2, then M1, and returns f1. Before KAFKA-20264, it returned j, the last parent of M2. R is now registered under f1.
 # {{maybeUpdateKeyChangingRepartitionNodeMap}} processes each merge node separately. R is downstream of both M1 and M2, and f1 is upstream of both. So both M1 and M2 take a copy of f1's set, and R goes into two sets.
 # {{mergeRepartitionTopics}} processes the M1 set first. It replaces R and removes R from its parents, so {{R.parentNodes()}} becomes empty.
 # It then processes the M2 set, which also contains R. {{findParentNodeMatching(R, ...)}} finds no parents and returns {{{}null{}}}, and the exception occurs.

Before KAFKA-20264, R was registered under j. M1 is not downstream of j, so only M2 took the set, and R was processed one time.
h3. Suggested fix

Make sure that each {{OptimizableRepartitionNode}} goes into only one merge node's set. Two possible ways:
 * In {{{}maybeUpdateKeyChangingRepartitionNodeMap{}}}, give each key changer's set only to the merge node nearest to the repartition nodes.
 * In {{{}mergeRepartitionTopics{}}}, skip a repartition node that has already been processed.

The tests that KAFKA-20264 added cover only a single merge. A test for nested merges would catch this regression.
h3. Workaround

Do not nest merges above a repartition. Merge all inputs at one merge node. The public API has only a two-input {{{}merge{}}}, so this requires a custom N-way merge.
fields.summary: Topology optimization fails with "Found a null keyChangingChild node" on nested merges

renderedFields.description:
Problem

When topology.optimization=all is set, StreamsBuilder.build() throws this exception for a topology with nested merges:

org.apache.kafka.streams.errors.StreamsException: Found a null keyChangingChild node for OptimizableRepartitionNode{ BaseRepartitionNode{... repartitionTopic='grp-repartition', ...} StreamsGraphNode{nodeName='grp-repartition-source', ..., parentNodes=[]} }

The failure occurs when all of these conditions are true:

  1. A key-changing operation feeds a merge (the inner merge).
  2. The inner merge feeds a second merge (the outer merge).
  3. An optimizable repartition (for example groupByKey().count()) follows the outer merge.
  4. No other key-changing operation sits between them.

The same topology builds without an error on 4.2.2 and earlier.

Reproduction

StreamsBuilder b = new StreamsBuilder();
KStream<String, String> f1 = b.<String, String>stream("a").selectKey((k, v) -> v);
KStream<String, String> f2 = b.<String, String>stream("b").selectKey((k, v) -> v);
KStream<String, String> j  = b.<String, String>stream("c").selectKey((k, v) -> v);

f1.merge(f2).merge(j)
  .groupByKey(Grouped.with("grp", Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()))
  .count();

Properties p = new Properties();
p.put(StreamsConfig.APPLICATION_ID_CONFIG, "repro");
p.put(StreamsConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "localhost:9092");
p.put(StreamsConfig.TOPOLOGY_OPTIMIZATION_CONFIG, StreamsConfig.OPTIMIZE);
b.build(p); // throws on 4.3.x and 4.4.0
Version Result
4.1.2 OK
4.2.2 OK
4.3.1 StreamsException
4.4.0 StreamsException

A single merge with three inputs (a merge node with three parents) builds without an error on 4.4.0.

Cause

KAFKA-20264 changed InternalStreamsBuilder.findParentNodeMatching. The method now returns the first match in a depth-first search. Before the change, it returned the result of the last parent. The change is correct, but it exposes a defect in maybeUpdateKeyChangingRepartitionNodeMap.

In the reproduction, M1 = f1.merge(f2), M2 = M1.merge(j), and R is the repartition node below M2.

  1. getKeyChangingParentNode(R) searches up through M2, then M1, and returns f1. Before KAFKA-20264, it returned j, the last parent of M2. R is now registered under f1.
  2. maybeUpdateKeyChangingRepartitionNodeMap processes each merge node separately. R is downstream of both M1 and M2, and f1 is upstream of both. So both M1 and M2 take a copy of f1's set, and R goes into two sets.
  3. mergeRepartitionTopics processes the M1 set first. It replaces R and removes R from its parents, so R.parentNodes() becomes empty.
  4. It then processes the M2 set, which also contains R. findParentNodeMatching(R, ...) finds no parents and returns null, and the exception occurs.

Before KAFKA-20264, R was registered under j. M1 is not downstream of j, so only M2 took the set, and R was processed one time.

Suggested fix

Make sure that each OptimizableRepartitionNode goes into only one merge node's set. Two possible ways:

  • In maybeUpdateKeyChangingRepartitionNodeMap, give each key changer's set only to the merge node nearest to the repartition nodes.
  • In mergeRepartitionTopics, skip a repartition node that has already been processed.

The tests that KAFKA-20264 added cover only a single merge. A test for nested merges would catch this regression.

Workaround

Do not nest merges above a repartition. Merge all inputs at one merge node. The public API has only a two-input merge, so this requires a custom N-way merge.

fields.description:
SimpleHeterogeneousAssignmentBuilder#build computes the assignment for each topic in the union of the members' subscriptions. A topic that no member subscribes to anymore is never visited, so a member whose existing assignment contains it gets its old partitions for that topic carried over into the new target assignment.

For the same reason, the {{else}} branch in {{TopicAssignmentPartialBuilder#revokeUnassignablePartitions}} that removes the topic is
unreachable, since {{topicId}} always comes from {{subscribedTopicIds}} there.

The homogeneous builder handles this case correctly: {{SimpleHomogeneousAssignmentBuilder}}
iterates over each member's existing assignment and removes topics that are no longer subscribed.

This behavior has been present since the builder was introduced by KAFKA-19363
(https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/20074), and is present in 4.2.0.

h3. Reproduction

Invoke {{SimpleAssignor#assign}} with the following group specification:

* Topics: T1 (4 partitions), T2 (2 partitions), T3 (2 partitions)
* Member A subscribes to {T1}, existing assignment {T1=[0], T2=[0]}
* Member B subscribes to {T1, T3}, existing assignment {T1=[1], T2=[1]}
* Subscription type: HETEROGENEOUS

Actual assignor output (one observed run):
{noformat}
A={T2=[0], T1=[0, 2]}
B={T2=[1], T1=[1, 3], T3=[0, 1]}
{noformat}

Expected result: T2 is revoked from both members.

h3. Impact

Since KAFKA-19431, {{ShareGroupAssignmentBuilder}} filters out topics outside each member's subscription when reconciling the target assignment into the member's current assignment, so these stale partitions are not passed on to members.

This filtering does not modify the stored target assignment. The stale entries can therefore
survive subsequent rebalances while the group remains heterogeneous and no member subscribes to the topic.

This was found while adding tests in https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23874, where it was confirmed as a bug in review (https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23874#issuecomment-6394163465).

survive subsequent rebalances while the group remains heterogeneous and no member subscribes to the topic.

SimpleHeterogeneousAssignmentBuilder#build computes the assignment for each topic in the union of the members' subscriptions. A topic that no member subscribes to anymore is never visited, so a member whose existing assignment contains it gets its old partitions for that topic carried over into the new target assignment.

For the same reason, the {{else}} branch in {{TopicAssignmentPartialBuilder#revokeUnassignablePartitions}} that removes the topic is
unreachable, since {{topicId}} always comes from {{subscribedTopicIds}} there.

The homogeneous builder handles this case correctly {{SimpleHomogeneousAssignmentBuilder}}
iterates over each member's existing assignment and removes topics that are no longer subscribed.

This behavior has been present since the builder was introduced by KAFKA-19363
(https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/20074), and is present in 4.2.0.

h3. Reproduction

Invoke {{SimpleAssignor#assign}} with the following group specification:

* Topics: T1 (4 partitions), T2 (2 partitions), T3 (2 partitions)
* Member A subscribes to {T1}, existing assignment {T1=[0], T2=[0]}
* Member B subscribes to {T1, T3}, existing assignment {T1=[1], T2=[1]}
* Subscription type: HETEROGENEOUS

Actual assignor output (one observed run):
{noformat}
A={T2=[0], T1=[0, 2]}
B={T2=[1], T1=[1, 3], T3=[0, 1]}
{noformat}

Since KAFKA-19431, {{ShareGroupAssignmentBuilder}} filters out topics outside each member's subscription when reconciling the target assignment into the member's current assignment, so these stale partitions are not passed on to members.

This filtering does not modify the stored target assignment. The stale entries can therefore
survive subsequent rebalances while the group remains heterogeneous and no member subscribes to the topic.

fields.description:
Kafka clients report latency and size only as an average and a maximum over the last 30 seconds. Both don't show how values are spread out during that time. One slow request can pull the average far from a typical one, and there's no way to get a p50 or p99, or to combine numbers across clients or over an hour.

We should propose a distribution API that lets clients count how many values fall into each range, so metrics backends such as Prometheus and OpenTelemetry can show real histograms and compute any percentile over any period.

fields.description:
With exactly_once_v2 and the classic group protocol, a Streams instance that cannot reach the group coordinator keeps its active task and keeps committing what its wall clock punctuator writes, while the group has already given the same task to another instance. Both instances write the same changelog partition and neither is fenced. If the cut off instance is then closed cleanly, it keeps its state directory, and on restart it restores only from its own checkpoint offset onwards. The other instance's records below that offset are never applied, so the store no longer matches its changelog.

Reproduced twice end to end with 4.4.0 clients against 4.3.0 brokers. Line numbers below are at 4.4.0, the same code is on trunk. The streams group protocol (KIP-1071) was not tested.

Why the instance keeps the task:
-> ConsumerCoordinator.poll calls pollHeartbeat (525), then returns early while the coordinator is unknown (526-528), before the rejoin check at 530. The task is never revoked or marked lost.
-> In the heartbeat thread (AbstractCoordinator 1513-1531) the coordinatorUnknown() branch only looks up the coordinator again and backs off. The session timeout branch at 1523 only marks the coordinator unknown, and the poll timeout leave at 1528 is an else-if after 1513, so it is not reached while the coordinator is unknown.

Why EOS does not fence it:
-> A punctuator only commit has no input offsets. TaskExecutor.commitOffsetsOrTransaction still commits because a transaction is in flight (181-186) and passes an empty map to StreamsProducer.commitTransaction, which calls sendOffsetsToTransaction (249).
-> KafkaProducer.sendOffsetsToTransaction only contacts the group coordinator when the map is not empty (800, from KAFKA-13319). The transaction commits against the transaction coordinator, which is still reachable, and group membership is never checked.
-> The two instances have different transactional ids, so they do not fence each other either. Their changelog records interleave.

Why the store stays wrong:
-> A clean close keeps the task directory. StateManagerUtil only wipes on an unclean close (168-169, 183-189; transactional state stores were off).
-> On restart ProcessorStateManager initialises the store offset from the store's own committed offset (334-338) and StoreChangelogReader seeks to that offset + 1 (1028-1032). Nothing below it is read again.

Setup:
# Three KRaft brokers. __consumer_offsets on broker 2, __transaction_state on broker 1, the input topic (1 partition) and the changelog on broker 3.
# Two instances A and B, exactly_once_v2, commit.interval.ms=100, session.timeout.ms=6000, heartbeat.interval.ms=2000, one persistent KeyValueStore, a 1 s wall clock punctuator that puts a new key each time. No input traffic.
# Blackhole the route from the instance that owns 0_0 (A) to broker 2 only. Within 30 s B has 0_0 active while A still reports 0_0 active, stays RUNNING and keeps punctuating.
# After one to two minutes close A cleanly (end of run in the first run, SIGTERM in the second). One "Closed clean", task directory kept.
# Restart A on the same state directory. Restore a third instance from an empty state directory as the reference.

Results:
||Run||A records in changelog||B records in changelog||A restarted from checkpoint||B keys in reference store||B keys in restarted A||Missing||
|1|208 (offsets 0 to 626)|554 (offsets 204 to 1522)|626|554|448|106, all at offsets 204 to 624|
|2|178 (offsets 0 to 522)|85 (offsets 188 to 524)|522|85|1|84, all at offsets 188 to 520|

Restarted A logs "State store store initialized from checkpoint with offset 626" (run 1) and restores from 627 on. A's own keys are all there. Nothing repairs this later since the checkpoint looks valid to Streams.

Not run, only follows from the same path: a key B deleted below A's checkpoint offset keeps A's old value after the restart.

What I think could be done: check group membership on the transactional commit even when there are no offsets to send, or treat a coordinator that stays unknown past the session timeout as losing the assignment, or let the poll timeout leave run outside the coordinatorUnknown() branch. Not sure which one fits best.

comments.body:
[~mjsax] Thanks , makes sense. I also checked whether an empty TxnOffsetCommit could do the job, but the broker answers it straight away without going to the group coordinator (same on 3.0 and 4.4), so we do need real offsets in there.

One thing to be careful about is which offset gets sent. If it's the consumer position, records that were fetched but not processed yet would be skipped after a failover. StreamTask.findOffsetAndMetadata already gives the head of the task's queue and committableOffsetsAndMetadata already commits all input partitions when processor metadata needs a commit. Maybe the same path can be reused when a task has writes under eos v2 but consumed nothing? Then the extra AddOffsetsToTxn/TxnOffsetCommit only happens in that case.

Yes, we would need to idempotently commit the same offset as before... Would need to check the code how to get the right value; don't know from top of my head. – To make the commit as lightweight as possible, we should also only include a minimum set of offset to be committed (ie, only one – I doubt that we could use an empty offset map? maybe worth to double check what `addOffsetsToTransaction(...)` would do with an empty map – also wondering if we could maybe allow/support empty map, just to get the check for the group membership).

[~mjsax] I had a look at what an empty map does, in case it helps.

On the producer side, if I read it right, sendOffsetsToTransaction returns straight away when the map is empty, so neither AddOffsetsToTxn nor TxnOffsetCommit goes out. That seems to have come in with KAFKA-13319 (3.1.0), to avoid markers piling up in __consumer_offsets.

On the broker side, KafkaApis.handleTxnOffsetCommitRequest looks like it answers a TxnOffsetCommit without topics by itself, without going to the group coordinator (I saw the same on 3.0 and trunk). So my understanding is that allowing an empty map would need a broker change too, and older brokers would still skip the check. Please correct me if I missed something there.

That makes me think one real offset might be the simpler route. From what I see the group coordinator validates member id and generation once per request (OffsetMetadataManager.commitTransactionalOffset), so one offset could already be enough for the check.

About the value, I wonder if StreamTask.findOffsetAndMetadata could be reused. It takes the head of the task's queue, or the next offset from the last fetch when the queue is empty, not the consumer position. If nothing was processed since the last commit, I think that comes out as the offset committed last time (maybe moved past control records), so the commit would be idempotent. It returns empty for a partition where nothing was fetched yet since the assignment, which might need some thought.

Just an idea, you know this code much better than me, so happy to be told if this doesn't hold .

??That would be a pickle... Maybe Justine Olshan can chime in? (Given that punctuations and EOS are in general kind of an anti-pattern, I would personally be ok to only fix for newer version is we need a broker change).??

Could I ask for your view on the anti-pattern point, since it's how we run expiry today? Two of our EOS v2 services keep a large key-value store (over 200 million keys in our load tests) whose entries have to go after a fixed retention say for ex 100 days ... A persistent key-value store has no TTL, and expiring at the RocksDB level would bypass the changelog, so the entries would come back after a restore. So we keep a second store as an expiry index (expiry bucket plus key) and a wall-clock punctuator every few minutes that range-scans it up to now and deletes from both stores through the store API, so both changelogs get the tombstones.

We already learned one lesson there: a cleanup run of 14 to 18 seconds held the transaction open past the 10 second transaction timeout, the producer got fenced and the task restored from scratch, again and again. Each run now has a time budget and keeps a watermark, so the next run picks up where the last one stopped.

What would you recommend instead? A stream-time punctuator or a bounded cleanup inside process() would commit input offsets together with the deletes, but both stop when a partition goes quiet. A periodic tick record per partition on an input topic would keep the cleanup running as normal processing... Is that the pattern you'd suggest, or is there something planned for TTL on key-value stores? (for us , expired entry cleanup is a pain at our volume). if there is a better place to have this discussion , we can do that too if you want .

fields.description:
With exactly_once_v2 and the classic group protocol, a commit that times out against the transaction coordinator can make Streams skip input records. The input offsets get committed past records that were never processed, so they never reach the store or the changelog.

When it happens: the commit has to fail with a TimeoutException while the transaction is still open at the coordinator. So transaction.timeout.ms has to be above the producer max.block.ms, and the transaction coordinator has to be unreachable for longer than max.block.ms. With the Streams EOS defaults (transaction.timeout.ms 10000, max.block.ms 60000) the coordinator aborts first, the next commit fails with InvalidTxnStateException and the thread dies, and I saw no loss. With transaction.timeout.ms=120000 and max.block.ms left at 60000, a 70 s outage was enough.

Reproduced on 4.2.1 and 4.4.0. Line numbers at 4.4.0, the same code is on trunk (not run on trunk). The streams group protocol was not tested; StreamThread only enforces the rebalance below when streamsRebalanceData is empty.

What happens:
-> The commit fails with "Timeout expired after 60000ms while awaiting EndTxn(true)" and TaskExecutor marks the task corrupted (188-200).
-> TaskManager.handleCorruption closes the task dirty, which drops the records it fetched but has not processed yet, adds the input partitions for an offset reset (TaskManager 320), revives the task and puts it in the tasks pending initialization (325).
-> StreamThread enforces a rebalance, "Active task(s) got corrupted. Triggering a rebalance." (1025-1027).
-> On the new assignment handleTasksPendingInitialization closes every task pending initialization (TaskManager 514-525), the revived one included, and a new StreamTask is created for the same task id. Its resetOffsetsForPartitions starts empty (StreamTask 198).
-> The seek back to the committed offset only runs for partitions in that set (StreamTask 1054-1069), so there is no seek. The new task starts at the consumer position and the next commit moves the input offset past the dropped records.

Setup:
# Three KRaft brokers. __transaction_state on broker 1, __consumer_offsets on broker 2, input topic (1 partition) and changelog on broker 3.
# One instance, one thread, exactly_once_v2, commit.interval.ms=100, producer transaction.timeout.ms=120000, max.block.ms default. A processor that puts every input record into a persistent KeyValueStore and sleeps 2 ms per record, so a commit lands in the middle of a fetched batch.
# Produce 24,000 records with unique keys f-0 to f-23999 at 200 per second.
# 40 s into the feed blackhole the route from the app to broker 1 only, for 70 s, then remove it.
# Compare the distinct keys in the changelog (read_committed) with the input, and the group's committed offset with the log end offset.

Results:
||Version||Old task last processed offset||New task first processed offset||Seek on the input after startup||Keys missing from the changelog||Group committed||
|4.4.0|8102|8200|none|97, f-8103 to f-8199|24,000 of 24,000|
|4.2.1|8055|8200|none|144, f-8056 to f-8199|24,000 of 24,000|

The same happened in 9 more runs with max.block.ms=3000, transaction.timeout.ms=60000 and two 6 s outages, on both versions, with one instance and with three instances on six partitions, and also without the processing delay. Those runs lost 39 to 365 records each. Runs without an outage lost nothing.

Two things that point at the lost reset rather than at the transaction:
-> In one run the revived task instance was initialized again instead of being replaced. The consumer logged "Seeking to offset 8223" and nothing was lost.
-> In a lossy run the changelog has the transaction of producer epoch 53 ending at f-8222 and the next one, epoch 54, starting at f-8400. f-8223 to f-8399 are in no batch at all and there is no abort marker, so they were never written. They were fetched, dropped by the dirty close, and skipped.

KAFKA-21159 on trunk clears the next offsets to consume on close so a revived task cannot commit a stale offset after the consumer is seeked back. Here the seek back never happens, so it does not cover this.

What I think could be done: keep the pending offset reset when handleTasksPendingInitialization closes a revived task, for example by carrying it into the new task, or seek those input partitions to their committed offsets when the revived task is closed.
fields.summary: Streams EOS: input records skipped after a commit timeout, the offset reset of the revived task is lost when the enforced rebalance closes it

comments.body:
Thanks [~zoro30102000] for raising this. I don't think we should allow {{transaction.timeout.ms}} to be greater than {{{}max.block.ms{}}}. The client gives up while the transaction is still open at the coordinator, which is an ambiguous state: the transaction might still commit or abort. We could add a check in \{{StreamsConfig }}and for now it would log a warning and fail at startup in the next major release.

That said, you've found a real bug that needs fixing however it's reached. When {{handleTasksPendingInitialization}} closes the revived task, the pending offset reset is lost, so the new task never seeks back to the committed offset.

 

We should get this addressed ASAP so I've assigned this to myself, but let me know if you'd like to the PR

renderedFields.description:
With exactly_once_v2 and the classic group protocol, a commit that times out against the transaction coordinator can make Streams skip input records. The input offsets get committed past records that were never processed, so they never reach the store or the changelog.

When it happens: the commit has to fail with a TimeoutException while the transaction is still open at the coordinator. So transaction.timeout.ms has to be above the producer max.block.ms, and the transaction coordinator has to be unreachable for longer than max.block.ms. With the Streams EOS defaults (transaction.timeout.ms 10000, max.block.ms 60000) the coordinator aborts first, the next commit fails with InvalidTxnStateException and the thread dies, and I saw no loss. With transaction.timeout.ms=120000 and max.block.ms left at 60000, a 70 s outage was enough.

Reproduced on 4.2.1 and 4.4.0. Line numbers at 4.4.0, the same code is on trunk (not run on trunk). The streams group protocol was not tested; StreamThread only enforces the rebalance below when streamsRebalanceData is empty.

What happens:
-> The commit fails with "Timeout expired after 60000ms while awaiting EndTxn(true)" and TaskExecutor marks the task corrupted (188-200).
-> TaskManager.handleCorruption closes the task dirty, which drops the records it fetched but has not processed yet, adds the input partitions for an offset reset (TaskManager 320), revives the task and puts it in the tasks pending initialization (325).
-> StreamThread enforces a rebalance, "Active task(s) got corrupted. Triggering a rebalance." (1025-1027).
-> On the new assignment handleTasksPendingInitialization closes every task pending initialization (TaskManager 514-525), the revived one included, and a new StreamTask is created for the same task id. Its resetOffsetsForPartitions starts empty (StreamTask 198).
-> The seek back to the committed offset only runs for partitions in that set (StreamTask 1054-1069), so there is no seek. The new task starts at the consumer position and the next commit moves the input offset past the dropped records.

Setup:

  1. Three KRaft brokers. __transaction_state on broker 1, __consumer_offsets on broker 2, input topic (1 partition) and changelog on broker 3.
  2. One instance, one thread, exactly_once_v2, commit.interval.ms=100, producer transaction.timeout.ms=120000, max.block.ms default. A processor that puts every input record into a persistent KeyValueStore and sleeps 2 ms per record, so a commit lands in the middle of a fetched batch.
  3. Produce 24,000 records with unique keys f-0 to f-23999 at 200 per second.
  4. 40 s into the feed blackhole the route from the app to broker 1 only, for 70 s, then remove it.
  5. Compare the distinct keys in the changelog (read_committed) with the input, and the group's committed offset with the log end offset.

Results:

Version Old task last processed offset New task first processed offset Seek on the input after startup Keys missing from the changelog Group committed
4.4.0 8102 8200 none 97, f-8103 to f-8199 24,000 of 24,000
4.2.1 8055 8200 none 144, f-8056 to f-8199 24,000 of 24,000

The same happened in 9 more runs with max.block.ms=3000, transaction.timeout.ms=60000 and two 6 s outages, on both versions, with one instance and with three instances on six partitions, and also without the processing delay. Those runs lost 39 to 365 records each. Runs without an outage lost nothing.

Two things that point at the lost reset rather than at the transaction:
-> In one run the revived task instance was initialized again instead of being replaced. The consumer logged "Seeking to offset 8223" and nothing was lost.
-> In a lossy run the changelog has the transaction of producer epoch 53 ending at f-8222 and the next one, epoch 54, starting at f-8400. f-8223 to f-8399 are in no batch at all and there is no abort marker, so they were never written. They were fetched, dropped by the dirty close, and skipped.

KAFKA-21159 on trunk clears the next offsets to consume on close so a revived task cannot commit a stale offset after the consumer is seeked back. Here the seek back never happens, so it does not cover this.

What I think could be done: keep the pending offset reset when handleTasksPendingInitialization closes a revived task, for example by carrying it into the new task, or seek those input partitions to their committed offsets when the revived task is closed.

comments.body:
Thanks zoro30102000 for raising this. I don't think we should allow transaction.timeout.ms to be greater than max.block.ms. The client gives up while the transaction is still open at the coordinator, which is an ambiguous state: the transaction might still commit or abort. We could add a check in {{StreamsConfig }}and for now it would log a warning and fail at startup in the next major release.

That said, you've found a real bug that needs fixing however it's reached. When handleTasksPendingInitialization closes the revived task, the pending offset reset is lost, so the new task never seeks back to the committed offset.

 

We should get this addressed ASAP so I've assigned this to myself, but let me know if you'd like to the PR

fields.description:
Tools that replicate consumer group offsets across clusters, such as MirrorMaker 2 and the group offset sync in KIP-1279, list groups using {{Admin.listGroups}} and then fetch their offsets using {{{}Admin.listConsumerGroupOffsets{}}}. In large deployments, many groups may have members but no committed offsets, resulting in unnecessary OffsetFetch processing and additional load on group coordinators.

This issue tracks KIP-1388, which proposes adding a request-side filter to the ListGroups API (version 6) and a corresponding {{ListGroupsOptions.requireCommittedOffsets(boolean)}} option. When enabled, the filter allows the server to return only groups with at least one committed offset, reducing unnecessary offset fetches.

KIP: [https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-1388%3A+Add+a+committed-offsets+filter+to+ListGroups]

Tools that replicate consumer group offsets between clusters (MirrorMaker 2, the group offset sync in KIP-1279, and others built on the Admin API) list every group with Admin.listGroups and then fetch offsets per group with Admin.listConsumerGroupOffsets. In large deployments thousands of groups have members but no committed offsets, so every OffsetFetch for them is wasted work on the group coordinators.

This ticket tracks the KIP that adds a request-side filter to the ListGroups API (version 6) and a matching ListGroupsOptions.requireCommittedOffsets(boolean) option, so that only groups with at least one committed offset are returned.
